checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: The Law of 22 Prairial was repealed and the Jacobin Club was closed; also leaders of the Paris Commune were arrested or executed and many Terror laws were rolled back.
checkpoint_questions.question: Quickly name two immediate legal or political changes that followed Robespierre's arrest and execution in July 1794.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: The law denied accused 'enemies of the people' normal rights to defense and limited evidence, which sped trials and made it easier for prosecutors to win convictions, producing a sharp rise in executions.
checkpoint_questions.question: Explain in one sentence how the Law of 22 Prairial changed trial rights and why that increased executions.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: It set up a bicameral legislature (Council of 500 and Council of Ancients) and a five-member executive (the Directory) chosen by indirect election with property qualifications, making government broader and less centralized.
checkpoint_questions.question: State one institutional change the Constitution of Year III created to prevent concentration of power.

entry_ticket.expected_response: A single choice (Convention / Parisians / army / Robespierre’s mistakes) plus one sentence explaining the choice. For example: “The Convention — members denounced and arrested Robespierre because his power and the Law of 22 Prairial alarmed other deputies.”
entry_ticket.prompt: Write one sentence answering: Who was responsible for ending the Reign of Terror — the Convention that arrested Robespierre, ordinary Parisians, the army, or Robespierre’s political mistakes? Pick the single best answer and give one short reason.

exit_ticket.prompt: In a short paragraph (about 6–8 sentences) analyze the causes and consequences of the Reign of Terror between 1793–1794 and explain why the Thermidorian Reaction followed. Use at least two specific pieces of evidence from this period.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: The response explains at least one cause of the Terror (e.g., political crisis, war, fear of internal enemies), cites the Law of 22 Prairial or increased executions as evidence of how the Terror operated, and connects Robespierre's arrest/execution plus the repeal of the Law of 22 Prairial to the Thermidorian Reaction; it then gives at least one consequence (e.g., roll-back of Terror measures, reprisals in the south, or creation of the Year III constitution/Directory) and links these consequences to efforts to limit concentrated power.

homework.submission_format: one-page typed essay and a photographed/scan of the handwritten chart uploaded to the classroom platform
tasks: Write a one-page (250–350 words) short essay that argues why the Law of 22 Prairial was a turning point in the Reign of Terror. Use two specific examples from class notes or the period summary to support your point.
Create a two-column chart (can be handwritten) listing three causes of the Reign of Terror on the left and three short-term consequences on the right, with one sentence explaining each link.

mentor_moment.story: A young clerk once told me he admired fast courts because they 'saved time.' When asked about one wrongful conviction later overturned, he admitted speed had hidden poor evidence and silenced witnesses.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Speed in trials can remove protections that prevent mistakes; reforms after the Terror show why legal rights matter even in crises.
mentor_moment.title: When a system pushes quick justice, mistakes grow

anticipated_questions: Can I change my entry ticket after I hand it in? (No — we’ll use these to start.)
Do we need full sentences? (Yes, but brief — pick one reason.)
Will you return the tickets? (No — I’ll keep them to note common ideas.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the lesson goal heading and a one-line objective.
teacher_script.heading: Collect entry tickets and set goal
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Ask students to put pens down. Say: “I’ll collect your one-sentence entry tickets — hand them up quickly.” As you collect, read aloud two contrasting answers (one blaming the Convention, one blaming Robespierre’s mistakes). Then say: “Today’s goal: by the end of class you should be able to explain why Robespierre fell and how that fall changed French government.” Point to the board heading you will write. "We will look at three pieces of evidence from this period and then try a short role-play to test who benefits from the Thermidorian changes."

anticipated_questions: Was Robespierre the only leader executed? (No — several colleagues were executed with him.)
Did the army arrest him? (No — he was denounced and arrested by deputies in the Convention.)
Why would deputies turn on him? (They feared his power and the consequences of the law; some historians say they acted to save themselves.)
Did executions stop immediately after his fall? (Not everywhere — there were revenge killings in parts of France.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write three numbered facts exactly: 1) Law of 22 Prairial (10 June 1794) — denied many accused the right to defend themselves; executions rose. 2) Arrest and execution of Robespierre — attempted suicide, arrested, executed 28 July 1794. 3) Aftermath — repeal of Law of 22 Prairial; Jacobin Club closed.
teacher_script.heading: Explain fall of Robespierre and Law of 22 Prairial
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: “I will read three short facts. Listen and follow on the board.” Read clearly: 1) “10 June 1794: Law of 22 Prairial — it removed the right of many accused to defend themselves, which increased executions in Paris.” Pause and ask: “Why would removing a right to defend increase executions?” Wait for answers; accept a range. 2) “July 1794: Members of the Convention denounced Robespierre; he attempted suicide, was arrested, and executed on 28 July with several allies.” Ask: “What does an arrest by the Convention tell us about who had power?” 3) “After his fall: the Law of 22 Prairial was repealed and the Jacobin Club closed.” Ask: “What immediate legal or political changes do those repeals create?” If a student mentions revenge killings in the south, say: “Yes — we’ll touch on regional violence next.”

anticipated_questions: What if I disagree with my role? (Stick to the role for the activity — we are testing arguments.)
Can we use examples from the provinces? (Yes — mention revenge killings if you know them.)
How long do we speak? (One line — 20 seconds max.)
teacher_script.board_action: Create three column headings: Convention deputies | Jacobin supporters | Worried moderates. Under each, write one student quote from the role-play and one bullet consequence noted by class.
teacher_script.heading: Structured role-play: Thermidorian Convention deputies
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Explain roles quickly: split class into three groups (Convention deputies, Jacobin supporters, worried moderates). Give each group 3 minutes to prepare one short line they would say on the convention floor (I will time you). Prompt each group: Convention deputies: explain why you vote to arrest Robespierre; Jacobin supporters: defend him; Worried moderates: explain how the Law of 22 Prairial made you afraid. After 3 minutes, invite one speaker from each group to deliver one line each (no more than 20 seconds). After the three lines, ask the class: “Which arguments helped the Convention majority justify arrest?” Write quick notes from their answers. If time remains, ask: “What consequences might the repeal of the law and closing of Jacobins have for local government and elections?”

anticipated_questions: Do we need to write full sentences? (Yes, brief and clear.)
What counts as a consequence? (Examples: more trials, more executions, fear in deputies, repeal later.)
Can we say 'unsure'? (Yes, but give a short reason.)
teacher_script.board_action: Project the three check sentences so every student can copy them.
teacher_script.heading: Check understanding: quick written prompt
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Hand out a 3-sentence exit check (or project it). Read it aloud: 1) Write one sentence: What was the Law of 22 Prairial and one consequence? 2) Write one sentence: Why did the Convention arrest Robespierre? 3) Circle whether the repeal of the law made France more or less likely to use state terror (circle: more / less / unsure) and give one reason. Give students 5 minutes to write. Collect answers.

anticipated_questions: What does 'indirect election' mean? (Voters chose electors who then chose deputies.)
Why property qualifications? (The Convention wanted to limit who could hold power; it was a reaction to popular democracy associated with the Terror.)
Did the Directory stop violence? (It reduced some legal instruments of terror but violence and unrest continued in places.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write: Constitution of Year III — Council of 500; Council of Ancients; Five-member Directory; deputies by indirect election; property qualifications.
teacher_script.heading: Consolidate and link to Constitution of Year III
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: “We’ve seen immediate legal changes after Thermidor — repeal of the Law of 22 Prairial and closing of the Jacobin Club. Now the Convention voted a new constitution in 1795. I will read two core facts and write them on the board.” Read and point: “The Constitution of Year III created a bicameral legislature: Council of 500 and Council of Ancients, and a five-member executive called the Directory. Deputies were chosen by indirect election with property qualifications.” Ask: “How might these changes reflect a reaction against the Terror?” Prompt answers: fewer concentrated powers, property rules to exclude the poorest, and indirect elections to reduce sudden popular pressure. End: “Next lesson we will use this to track how the Directory faced military and economic issues.”

bullet_points: Mobilisation (conscription) from 1792 → large citizen armies
Major battles: Valmy, Jemappes (showed French army strength)
Territorial changes by 1795: annexed Austrian Netherlands; Batavian Republic established
Directory (after Constitution of Year III): unrest, economic weakness, corruption
Directory often used the army to resolve political deadlocks → pattern leading to coups (e.g. 18 Brumaire)
4 Feb 1794: Convention voted to abolish slavery and grant full rights in colonies
Commissioners in Saint-Domingue began emancipations before 1794 — implementation across colonies was uneven
Newspapers and pamphlets: key to debate — 130+ in 1789; 2,000+ in the 1790s
diagrams_to_draw: Simple map: north-eastern France with Valmy and Jemappes labelled; arrow to Austrian Netherlands and Batavian Republic
Three-column quick chart: Law in Paris | Actions in colonies | Effect (example: 4 Feb 1794 | Saint-Domingue commissioners | uneven implementation)
headings: Today: Wars, Directory, and Colonial Emancipation

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Conscription mobilised large numbers of soldiers quickly to defend the Revolution and fight abroad. It let France field bigger armies, win battles like Valmy and Jemappes, and by 1795 annex territories such as the Austrian Netherlands and set up allied republics (e.g., the Batavian Republic).
checkpoint_questions.question: Why did France introduce mass conscription during the Revolutionary Wars, and how did that affect France’s position by 1795?

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Example: the Directory relied on military force to put down uprisings and resolve political deadlocks (it depended on generals and interventions). This shows a weakness: limited popular legitimacy and political instability; and a strength: the army kept the government in power until 18 Brumaire.
checkpoint_questions.question: Give one clear example of how the Directory used the army in politics, and explain what that shows about the Directory’s strengths or weaknesses.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: The Convention abolished slavery in the colonies and granted full rights regardless of colour. Commissioners in Saint-Domingue had already begun emancipating enslaved people before the national vote, so local actions pushed the national decision and show that emancipation was already happening on the ground.
checkpoint_questions.question: What did the Convention’s 4 February 1794 vote change in the colonies, and why does the text say commissioners in Saint-Domingue mattered earlier?

entry_ticket.expected_response: False. The Convention voted to abolish slavery on 4 Feb 1794 and granted rights, but some emancipations began earlier in Saint-Domingue and implementation across colonies was uneven and contested.
entry_ticket.prompt: True or false? France permanently ended slavery across all its colonies on 4 February 1794. Briefly explain your answer in one sentence.

exit_ticket.prompt: Write a focused paragraph (5–8 sentences) that analyses two main causes of the Reign of Terror (1793–1794), two major consequences for French politics or society, and explains why the Thermidorian Reaction followed the Terror.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Paragraph names at least two causes (for example: foreign war and internal factional struggle or Committee policies), describes at least two consequences (for example: mass executions/political purges and political backlash leading to fear of radical rule), and explains the connection to Thermidor (for example: elite and political leaders reacted to excesses and legal changes, removing Robespierre and creating the Directory/Constitution of Year III).

homework.submission_format: Hand in the chart and paragraph (paper or photo) and bring the annotated excerpt to class.
tasks: Make a one-page two-column chart titled 'Causes' and 'Consequences' of the Reign of Terror. Put at least three items under each column and add one sentence under each item explaining its importance (30 minutes).

Choose one of the three Directory challenges discussed in class (political unrest, economic weakness, or corruption). Write a one-paragraph explanation of how the Directory tried to cope with it and whether using the army helped or hurt (20 minutes).

Locate (teacher will supply) a short newspaper or pamphlet excerpt from the 1790s and annotate it with two questions about who wrote it and what audience it aimed for; bring the annotated excerpt to the next lesson (15 minutes).

mentor_moment.story: A young clerk copied a popular pamphlet and handed it to soldiers leaving for the front; the pamphlet shaped how they talked about rights and the enemy when they returned home.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Prints and pamphlets reached ordinary people quickly; thinking about who wrote a source and who read it helps you judge its political effect.
mentor_moment.title: When a pamphlet changed a debate

anticipated_questions: If the Convention voted it, why wouldn’t it be permanent?
Was Saint-Domingue the same as other colonies?
Will we cover Robespierre again?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the lesson purpose (short). Copy one short student sentence from each example (True/False).
teacher_script.heading: Collect entry tickets and set learning purpose
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Read one or two student answers aloud (pick one that says True and one that says False). Say: “We asked about abolition on 4 February 1794. The Convention did vote to abolish slavery then and to give full rights in theory. But what actually happened in the colonies was more complicated. Today we will look at three connected areas: the wars and mobilisation, how the Directory governed at home, and what happened to slavery in the colonies. By the end I want you to be able to explain why the Terror ended and why Thermidor followed, using evidence.”

anticipated_questions: Did conscription apply to everyone or just volunteers?
Were Valmy and Jemappes both French victories?
How did annexation work — did local people agree?
teacher_script.board_action: Draw a simple map of north-eastern France, label Valmy, Jemappes; note dates 1792. Write short bullets about conscription, territorial annexations (Austrian Netherlands, Batavian Republic by 1795).
teacher_script.heading: Introduce the French Revolutionary Wars and mobilisation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: “Quick reminder: from 1792 the Revolution moved to total war. Use the whiteboard map I will draw. Ask: What does conscription or mobilisation mean for a country?” Wait for answers, then draw. Say: “Examples: major battles like Valmy and Jemappes showed revolutionary armies could win. By 1795 France had annexed neighbouring territories such as the Austrian Netherlands and created sister republics like the Batavian Republic.” Ask: “How might large-scale mobilisation change politics at home?” Prompt answers that link army power to politics.

anticipated_questions: Was corruption everywhere or only in the Directory?
What exactly was 18 Brumaire?
Did people support using the army to restore order?
teacher_script.board_action: Write bullets: Unrest; Economic weakness; Corruption; Use of army to resolve deadlock; Leads toward coups (18 Brumaire).
teacher_script.heading: Explain Directory problems and evidence of army influence
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: “The Directory began after the Constitution of Year III in 1795. It faced unrest and economic weakness. I will list specific problems and we will add evidence from sources.” Write on the board: unrest, economic weakness, corruption, reliance on army. Read aloud one short quote from a Directory-era newspaper (teacher reads a supplied short line: ‘The city is restless; troops keep order.’). Then ask: “How does that quote show reliance on the army?” Call on 2 students. Then say: “The Directory used military interventions to solve political deadlocks; this pattern of using the army helped lead to later coups, including 18 Brumaire.” Ask: “What are the dangers when a government often uses the military to settle politics?”

anticipated_questions: Does earlier emancipation in Saint-Domingue mean the colony was free before 1794?
Which source is more reliable — Paris or the commissioners?
Did all colonies react the same way?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the group task prompt and label the two sources: (A) Convention vote 4 Feb 1794; (B) Commissioners in Saint-Domingue emancipating earlier.
teacher_script.heading: Group discussion and source comparison: abolition in practice
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Arrange students in groups of three. Give each group a short prompt to compare two pieces of evidence I read: (A) the Convention’s vote on 4 Feb 1794 that abolished slavery and granted rights; (B) a report that commissioners in Saint-Domingue had begun emancipations before 1794. Task: In three minutes list one similarity and one difference about how emancipation reached people. Circulate and listen. After 3 minutes, ask two groups to share their similarity and difference. Emphasize: “These two pieces show competing perspectives: legal decree in Paris vs earlier actions in the colonies.”

After that, we will decide: did the Directory mostly use laws, money, or the army to solve problems?” Run the three short speeches, then lead the vote and ask students for evidence from today’s notes. bullet_points: Student examples: La Marseillaise — united people; Guillotine — cruelty; Cockade — Paris identity
La Marseillaise: A song composed in 1792 by Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle, adopted by the National Convention as the First Republic's anthem in 1795.
Guillotine: An execution device invented during the Revolution, celebrated by the left as the people's avenger and cursed by the right as the symbol of the Terror; it became a public spectacle.
Assignats: Paper currency backed by nationalised church and émigré lands used during the Revolution; excessive issuance contributed to hyperinflation.
Liberty cap (Phrygian cap): A brimless, felt conical cap with the tip pulled forward, symbolising Roman republicanism and liberty.
Role and repression of women: Women participated in activism and societies early, but 1791 and 1793 constitutions denied political rights; October 1793 banned women's clubs.

Worked example chain: 1) Confiscation of church & émigré lands → 2) Issue assignats backed by lands → 3) Excess issuance + poor harvests → 4) Inflation, price controls, black markets → withdrawal of assignats (1796).
Debate evidence (Symbols): La Marseillaise adoption (1795); cockade & liberty cap; guillotine as public spectacle and symbol.
Debate evidence (Economics): Assignats issued against confiscated lands; excessive issuance caused hyperinflation; price controls and black markets followed.
Final summary: Symbols had contested meanings (could unite or terrify). Assignats produced real economic hardship when over-issued.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Positive view: the left celebrated the guillotine as 'the people's avenger' (shows it could be seen as justice). Negative view: the right cursed it as the symbol of the Terror (shows it was also seen as cruelty).

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Confiscation of church and émigré lands backed assignats, but excessive issuance of assignats plus poor harvests increased the money supply and reduced confidence, producing hyperinflation, black markets, and price controls.

entry_ticket.prompt: Quick: write one sentence answering both parts. 1) Name one symbol or song from the French Revolution you know. 2) Say in one short phrase what that symbol made people feel or do (for example: 'made them feel proud' or 'made them fear the government').

teacher_script.speaker_notes: Ask students to hold up their sentence. Say: 'I will call three students with different answers.' anticipated_questions: Was La Marseillaise actually used by everyone? (It was adopted by the National Convention in 1795 and widely used as a revolutionary song — but not everyone agreed with it.)
Who invented the guillotine? (We use the defined term 'an execution device invented during the Revolution' — details of the inventor are for later study.)
Were cockades the same everywhere in France? (The blue-and-red cockade is linked to Paris, but local colors varied.)
teacher_script.board_action: Under the earlier three examples, add five short definition headings (one line each) as you read them.
teacher_script.heading: Introduce core definitions and contested meanings
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'We will run through five definitions from the chapter. I will read each definition aloud. If you disagree, raise your hand.' Read each definition exactly as written on your sheet: La Marseillaise; Guillotine; Assignats; Liberty cap (Phrygian cap); Cockade (blue-and-red of Paris) and the role of women briefly. After each definition ask: 'Is this new or surprising?' Pause for 10 seconds. Then say: 'Notice the guillotine line says it was both celebrated by the left and cursed by the right. That shows symbols can have opposite meanings.'

anticipated_questions: Did assignats have any value at first? (Yes; they were backed by confiscated lands, so they had value initially.)
Why did poor harvests matter? (They reduced food supply, pushing prices up while more money chased less food.)
Could the government have stopped inflation sooner? (The text says excessive issuance and other pressures produced hyperinflation; policy choices mattered.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw a four-step arrow chain on the board with each step written: 1) Confiscation of lands → 2) Issue assignats → 3) Excess issuance + poor harvests → 4) Inflation, price controls, black markets, withdrawal (1796).
teacher_script.heading: Worked example: assignats → inflation (guided)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'Now we will walk through the worked example from the chapter. I will draw a simple chain of events. Tell me if each step follows. Step 1: nationalise church and émigré lands. Step 2: issue assignats backed by those lands. Step 3: issue too many assignats and poor harvests happen. Step 4: prices rise; people use black markets; assignats are withdrawn in 1796.' Draw each step and ask the class after each step: 'Does this follow? If not, why not?' Call on students who raised hands. Emphasize causal words: because, led to, and contributed. Ask: 'Which steps are causes and which are effects?'

anticipated_questions: Can a person use both symbol and economic evidence? (For this task, pick one side but you can mention the other briefly if you want to be persuasive.)
What counts as evidence? (A fact from the chapter or the worked example is evidence.)
How long should our statements be? (Two short sentences: one evidence, one consequence.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the two debate positions as headings and list the two evidence bullets under each heading.
teacher_script.heading: Prepare students for role-play positions
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'You will role-play brief debates. Half the class argues that symbols (songs, caps, cockades, the guillotine) mostly shaped public opinion for the better (mobilized people, spread ideas). The other half argues that economic hardship from assignats and price controls mattered more for how people reacted. I will give each group two pieces of evidence to use from the chapter.' Hand out (or read aloud) two pieces of evidence per side: Symbols side: La Marseillaise adoption (1795) and use of cockade/liberty cap in public; Guillotine as a public spectacle. Economy side: Assignats chain of events, inflation and withdrawal in 1796, price controls and black markets. Ask groups to pick a spokesperson and prepare two short statements (one evidence sentence and one consequence sentence). Give one minute to discuss quietly in groups.

anticipated_questions: Can we quote the guillotine both as symbol and as policy? (You can say it's a symbol; the policy use is part of why it became symbolic.)
Do we have to stick to exactly the words from the chapter? (Use the chapter's facts — you can rephrase.)
What if nobody in my group wants to speak? (Pick one person quietly or share the speaking; the spokesperson can read the group's prepared lines.)
teacher_script.board_action: During debate, tick off which evidence each side uses by marking a check next to the bullet they mention.
teacher_script.heading: Structured role-play/debate
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'We will run a timed debate. Each side has 90 seconds to give their two statements. Then a 60-second rebuttal from the other side. After rebuttals, I will ask two quick questions to the class.' Use a visible timer. Call the symbols side first: the spokesperson gives evidence from the board and links it to public perception. Then the economy side responds with their evidence (assignats). Then each side gives a 60-second rebuttal. After both rebuttals ask the class: 'Which single piece of evidence changed your mind, if any?' Ask two students to explain briefly.

anticipated_questions: Will we study the guillotine or assignats more later? (Yes — both are next units.)
Do these summaries mean one side is right? (No — the text shows both mattered; our job is to weigh evidence.)
What should I review tonight? (Read the definitions and the assignats worked example.)
teacher_script.board_action: Under the debate headings, add one final summary sentence: 'Symbols: contested meanings. Assignats: caused inflation and hardship.'
teacher_script.heading: Check for understanding and consolidate
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'Final check: write one short line on a post-it or in your notes answering this: Name one piece of evidence that shows symbols shaped public opinion, and name one piece of evidence that shows economics shaped people's lives. Hand them to me or hold them up.' After collecting, read two examples aloud: one from each side. Close by summarizing: 'Symbols like La Marseillaise, cockades, and the liberty cap were powerful and had contested meanings; the guillotine was both symbol and spectacle. Assignats began as land-backed currency, but excessive issuance and poor harvests produced inflation and hardship.'

entry_ticket.expected_response: Correct choices: A and C. A is true: assignats were issued after confiscations. C is true: symbols influenced public perception. Common wrong choices: B is wrong because inflation had several causes including over-issuance and poor harvests, not just foreign acceptance. D is wrong because historians have written about the guillotine as a subject (see Opie).
entry_ticket.prompt:
Quick choice (2 minutes): Which two statements are true about assignats and symbols during the Revolution? Circle two.

A. Assignats were paper money created after the government seized church and émigré land.
B. Assignats caused inflation only because foreign governments refused to accept them.
C. Symbols like the cockade and La Marseillaise helped shape how people saw the Revolution.
D. The guillotine was only a symbol and was never written about as an object of study.

Write the two letters you choose and one short reason (one sentence) for one of your choices.

teacher_script.heading: Introduce new material: long-term impacts & bibliography
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: “Today we move from symbols and crisis to long-term effects and how historians study them. I will read three short claims from the chapter; after each claim, I’ll ask you to raise your hand if you think it’s supported by evidence in the chapter. Claim 1: ‘The Revolution ended feudalism in France.’ Raise your hand. Claim 2: ‘The Revolution promoted individual freedoms and influenced constitutions in other countries.’ Raise your hand. Claim 3: ‘Napoleonic legal codes were a main way the Revolution’s ideas spread across Europe.’ Raise your hand.” Pause after each and nod. Then say: “All three are supported, but historians disagree about how complete those changes were and how long they lasted. We also have a bibliography listing works on the guillotine and assignats — that means scholars have debated these topics in detail.” Show the example from the source: “Worked example — confiscation → assignats → over-issuance + poor harvests → inflation.” Point to the board flow-chart you will draw next.

teacher_script.speaker_notes: Divide the class into three groups and assign roles: Group A = argue that the Revolution created lasting change; Group B = argue that change was limited and reversed later; Group C = historians’ critics who point to specific evidence (e.g. rural continuities, inflation). Give 2 minutes to plan. Prompt: “Use one piece of evidence from the chapter or the bibliography example. For instance: point to the Napoleonic codes as evidence for lasting change, or point to inflation and social unrest as limits.” After planning, run three 2-minute mini-debates: Group A speaks, Group B responds, Group C asks one critical question. If time allows, swap speakers. Circulate, listen, and when each group finishes, ask one quick follow-up: “Which source would you cite from the bibliography to back your point?”

learning_objectives.statement: Recall the commonly given start and end dates of the French Revolution and cite the document's phrasing.
Explain how social, economic and political factors combined to produce a crisis that led to the calling of the Estates General in 1789, using evidence from the text.
Analyze the causes and consequences of the Reign of Terror between 1793 and 1794, and summarize why the Thermidorian Reaction followed.
Apply evidence from the chapter to describe two ways newspapers or symbols (e.g. La Marseillaise, the cockade) influenced public perception during the Revolution.

misconceptions.correction: The document shows the guillotine was both 'the principal symbol of the Terror' and celebrated on the left as 'the people's avenger', indicating contested cultural meanings.

evidence.quote: The guillotine remains "the principal symbol of the Terror in the French Revolution."
It was celebrated on the left as the people's avenger, for example in the revolutionary song La guillotine permanente , and cursed as the symbol of the Terror by the right.

misconceptions.statement: The guillotine was perceived only as a symbol of cruelty and the Terror.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Students may conflate the guillotine exclusively with executions during the Terror and ignore contemporary left-wing cultural references.

misconceptions.correction: Although women participated initially and organized societies, the 1791 and 1793 constitutions denied them political rights and women's clubs were banned in October 1793.

evidence.quote: Deprived of political rights by the Ancien Régime , the Revolution initially allowed women to participate, although only to a limited degree.
Despite this, the 1791 and 1793 constitutions denied them political rights and democratic citizenship.
the male-dominated Jacobins who then controlled the government denounced the Society as dangerous rabble-rousers and made all women's clubs and associations illegal.

misconceptions.statement: Women had equal political rights and full inclusion throughout the Revolution.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Early visible activism by women (pamphlets, demonstrations) can lead students to overgeneralize their influence across the Revolution's entire span.

prerequisites.statement: Basic familiarity with late-18th-century European monarchies and the notion of estates (clergy, nobility, Third Estate).
Understanding of simple economic terms (debt, inflation, taxation) as used in historical analysis.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: They called the Estates-General only because the government had no money left and needed to raise new taxes to pay off debts.
diagnostic_questions.question: Which of these statements best explains why the French monarchy called the Estates-General in 1788–1789?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Whether the student attributes the convocation solely to fiscal collapse or recognises a mixture of fiscal, political and social pressures (including elite resistance to reform and demand for political change).

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: The failing royal budget — once the state went bankrupt people had nothing to lose and that alone caused the popular uprisings.
diagnostic_questions.question: Which factor was the main cause of the popular unrest in 1789: rising bread prices, Enlightenment ideas, resistance by the nobility to reform, or the failing royal budget? Explain your choice in one sentence.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Whether the student reduces the Revolution to a single, immediate cause (economic collapse) instead of recognising that unrest drew on several interacting causes and differing local triggers.

learning_gaps.misconception: The French Revolution happened simply because the government ran out of money — once the state was bankrupt, people revolted and the Revolution followed directly.

remediation.action: Source-comparison carousel (30 minutes): students rotate through 4 short primary-source stations (a minister's fiscal report, a peasant petition about rents, an urban artisan letter about bread prices, and a noble's memorandum rejecting reform). At each station they answer two prompts: 'What problem does this source highlight?' and 'Who benefits from/loses by the current system?'
remediation.rationale: Confronts the student with simultaneous, distinct pieces of evidence that point to fiscal, social, economic and political causes. By asking about beneficiaries/losers, students must link structural interests to motivations, breaking the single-cause narrative and showing how different groups experienced crises differently.

remediation.action: Structured evidence-weighting task (20 minutes): give students a short list of causes (debt/fiscal crisis, social inequality of the estates, resistance of elite to reform, food shortages, political ideas) and a timeline of events 1786–1789. In pairs they place each cause on a 'short-term / long-term' continuum and write one piece of evidence from the sources/timeline that supports its placement.
remediation.rationale: Forces students to distinguish immediate triggers from deep-seated causes and to justify their judgements with evidence. This addresses the tendency to conflate chronology with sole causation and trains students to treat 'cause' as multi-layered and contingent.

remediation.action: Mini-debate with competing interpretations (25 minutes): split the class into three groups representing different historians' arguments (economic/financial interpretation, socio-political/estate-conflict interpretation, and ideological/cultural interpretation). Each group prepares two evidence-based points and one concession (a piece of evidence that supports another view) and then presents to the class.
remediation.rationale: Models the discipline's practice of weighing competing interpretations grounded in evidence, teaches students that historians disagree, and requires them to use primary evidence to defend a nuanced view rather than restating a simple, single-cause story.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: It just shows how cruel the Revolution was and that everyone feared the guillotine.
diagnostic_questions.question: Look at a caricature from 1793 showing a crowded square around a guillotine with a banner praising popular justice. What does this source most likely tell us about how at least some contemporaries viewed the guillotine?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If the student answers that it only shows fear and cruelty, they are treating all evidence about the guillotine as evidence of a single negative meaning rather than recognising contested contemporary attitudes.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: The ledger — both sources just prove how many people were killed; nothing celebrates the guillotine.
diagnostic_questions.question: Which of these two contemporary texts would best support the claim that some revolutionaries celebrated the guillotine as a symbol of popular justice: (A) a ledger of executions listing names and dates, or (B) a revolutionary song praising the 'people's avenger' and the fall of aristocrats? Explain briefly.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: A student holding the misconception will favour the ledger or claim both only support cruelty, failing to recognise sources that express positive or celebratory meanings.

evidence.quote: The guillotine remains "the principal symbol of the Terror in the French Revolution."
It was celebrated on the left as the people's avenger, for example in the revolutionary song La guillotine permanente , and cursed as the symbol of the Terror by the right.

learning_gaps.misconception: The guillotine was only a symbol of cruelty and the Terror — people only associated it with mass executions and fear.

remediation.action: Show students two primary sources side by side: an execution register or eyewitness account emphasizing deaths and terror, and a left-wing pamphlet or popular song from the 1790s that praises the guillotine as 'the people's avenger.' Ask small groups to list what each source is doing (information, persuasion, celebration) and to annotate language or images that signal tone.
remediation.rationale: Placing contrasting contemporaneous evidence together makes visible that the guillotine carried multiple meanings. Annotating persuasive language versus factual recording forces students to use evidence to infer attitudes rather than rely on present-day labels.

remediation.action: Run a short source-provenance activity: for the same celebratory pamphlet, have students identify the author/audience/purpose and then ask whether that provenance would make the pamphlet reliable for claiming general public opinion. Then repeat for a repression-focused source. Lead a class discussion on how social position and purpose shape portrayals.
remediation.rationale: Teaching provenance shows why different groups produced different representations — political actors sometimes promoted the guillotine positively. This addresses the root error (overgeneralisation) by helping students weigh sources rather than assume a single cultural meaning.

remediation.action: Conclude with a short comparative writing task: give students two minutes to write a one-sentence claim about what the guillotine symbolised, then two pieces of evidence (one fear-based, one celebratory) supporting a qualified claim that acknowledges contestation.
remediation.rationale: Forcing students to craft a nuanced claim with paired evidence moves them from a binary view to a contextualised interpretation grounded in texts, matching the lesson’s emphasis on competing interpretations and causation.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: There were hundreds or thousands of prisoners, which shows it was a huge popular liberation and the main thing that toppled the king.
diagnostic_questions.question: How many prisoners were being held in the Bastille on 14 July 1789, and why does that number matter for understanding the event?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Whether the student treats the storming as a large-scale liberation of many oppressed people (symbolic, decisive cause) rather than a politically symbolic attack on royal authority with limited immediate practical effect.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: Yes — the Assembly became revolutionary instantly after the Bastille, passed radical laws right away and the king lost his power immediately.
diagnostic_questions.question: Did the National Assembly immediately replace the monarchy and pass all its radical reforms the day after the Bastille was stormed? Explain briefly.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Whether the student assumes a single event produced instant, comprehensive political change instead of recognising a sequence of actions, negotiations and regional variations after 14 July.

learning_gaps.misconception: The Storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789 was the single decisive event that caused the French Revolution — once the Bastille was taken everything became revolutionary and the monarchy fell immediately.

remediation.action: Begin a 15-minute source comparison: give students three brief primary extracts (a Parisian eyewitness account emphasising fear and symbolism, the Bastille prison register listing seven prisoners, and a page from the June–August 1789 timeline of laws and protests). In pairs, students answer: which sources show symbolism, which show limited immediate effect, and which show ongoing political steps?
remediation.rationale: Confronting a striking eyewitness narrative with documentary facts (prison register) and the legislative timeline forces students to separate dramatic symbolism from material effect and to see change as a sequence. This directly addresses the over-generalisation from dramatic images to causal certainty.

remediation.action: Run a 20-minute structured sequencing activity: provide cards describing events and conditions (food shortages, Estates-General, Storming of the Bastille, formation of the National Guard, abolition of feudal privileges, royal resistance). Students work in small groups to place cards into 'causes', 'symbolic events', and 'consequences', then justify one placement to the class with textual evidence.
remediation.rationale: Making students categorize and justify shows that the Bastille is best understood as a symbolic trigger within a broader set of causes and consequences; requiring textual evidence prevents reliance on memory of a single dramatic date.

remediation.action: Conclude with a 10-minute comparative reflection: present two historians' short arguments (one emphasizing the Bastille as decisive symbol, another seeing it as one event among many structural causes). Ask students to write one paragraph weighing both interpretations and citing the primary evidence they've seen.
remediation.rationale: Presenting competing interpretations models historical practice and asks students to weigh evidence rather than accept a single narrative; this addresses the tendency to accept a simple causal story from dramatic imagery.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: Each deputy had an equal vote, so because the Third Estate had most deputies they could outvote the others and simply declare a new assembly.
diagnostic_questions.question: When the Estates-General met in May–June 1789, how were votes decided between the three Estates (clergy, nobility, Third Estate)?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: A student who answers incorrectly treats the Estates-General as if it already practised 'one deputy, one vote' and therefore believes the Third Estate had an immediate majority and so could legitimately 'leave' to form a government.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: They just stood up, walked out of the Estates-General, and immediately declared themselves the National Assembly to take power.
diagnostic_questions.question: Which best describes how representatives of the Third Estate became the National Assembly in June 1789?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: A wrong answer shows the student thinks the change was instantaneous and unilateral rather than the result of mandates from local electors, shifting alliances, and repeated disputes over procedure.

learning_gaps.misconception: The Third Estate just walked out of the Estates-General and immediately seized control by declaring themselves the National Assembly — it was a single dramatic break where the commoners decided to take power.

remediation.action: Begin the lesson with paired primary-source reading: excerpts from (a) deputies' cahiers and instructions to Third Estate delegates, (b) the August 1788 royal summons and rules for the Estates-General, and (c) the June 17, 1789 proclamation of the National Assembly. Ask pairs to list what each source says about who can decide votes, who the deputies represent, and whether deputies were told to form a new body.
remediation.rationale: Comparing the actual instructions and proclamations makes visible the legal ambiguity and local mandates that constrained deputies. This addresses the root: students' simplified narrative by forcing them to confront contemporary evidence that the move was negotiated and grounded in electoral mandates, not a single unilateral seizure.

remediation.action: Run a short classroom role-play of the Estates-General rules: assign groups as clergy, nobles, and Third Estate with realistic numbers of deputies and written 'mandates' (some instructing to insist on estate voting, others to demand head-count voting). Play two rounds—one with 'voting by order' and one with 'voting by head'—then simulate the debate over whether the Third Estate can meet separately and why some clergy/nobles join them.
remediation.rationale: Experiencing how different voting procedures change outcomes and how mandates limit delegates helps students see why deputies negotiated and why some members of the other Estates joined the Third Estate. This corrects the false image of an immediate, uncontested takeover by showing the procedural and political complexity.

remediation.action: Show a short timeline activity: students place dated excerpts (royal summons, meetings, the stalemate over voting, the Tennis Court Oath, deputies of some clergy/nobles joining) on a timeline and write one sentence about causation between each event. Conclude with a class discussion presenting competing interpretations from historians (e.g., sudden coup vs. gradual constitutional assertion).
remediation.rationale: Making the sequence explicit and weighing competing historical interpretations prevents readers from collapsing events into a single dramatic moment and reinforces that the National Assembly emerged through a sequence of disputes, local mandates, and changing alliances rather than a simple walkout.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: A) The meeting would have happened anyway because economic pressure made it inevitable.
diagnostic_questions.question:
Two rival pamphlets appear in a city within the same week: one argues the assembly should form immediately and gives meeting places and names of speakers; the other argues for patience and staying home. Within a month a mass meeting happens at the places the first pamphlet named and local leaders named in it speak. Which of the following is the best explanation?
A) The meeting would have happened anyway because economic pressure made it inevitable. B) The first pamphlet played an active role by persuading and coordinating people who then organised the meeting.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Whether the student recognises print as an active organizer and persuasive agent rather than a neutral reporter; a wrong answer shows they downplay the causal role of print in shaping events.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: A) The paper simply reported demonstrations others planned.
diagnostic_questions.question:
Historians find that a radical newspaper had a sudden rise in subscribers just before a wave of demonstrations and that the paper named meeting dates and slogans. Which interpretation best fits the evidence?
A) The paper simply reported demonstrations others planned. B) The paper likely helped coordinate people by spreading slogans and practical information, so it contributed to the demonstrations.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Whether the student uses timing and content evidence to infer active influence; a wrong answer shows they assume print only reflects events, not helps cause them.

learning_gaps.misconception: Newspapers and pamphlets just reported what was already happening — they were neutral, marginal sources that didn't shape the Revolution; the Revolution was caused by economic and social conditions, not by print culture.

remediation.action: Bring two short primary sources to class: a pamphlet/newspaper editorial that calls readers to a specific action (naming time/place/slogan) and a neutral-looking market report from the same month. Ask students in pairs to identify differences in audience, language, and intended effect, then map how the call-to-action could reach people in that city.
remediation.rationale: Comparing contemporaneous primary texts makes the persuasive and organising features of print visible (naming places, giving instructions, using emotive rhetoric). This addresses the root error — seeing all print as neutral — by letting students read the evidence that some print deliberately sought to mobilise.

remediation.action: Present a short timeline with dates for pamphlet publications, newspaper circulation spikes, and subsequent local events (meetings, protests). Ask students to construct two competing interpretations (print caused the events vs print only reported them) and pick which the evidence better supports, citing specific timeline links.
remediation.rationale: Making students weigh competing interpretations grounded in chronological evidence trains them to see causal plausibility — when persuasive print precedes and provides details for events, it is reasonable to infer influence. This directly counters the tendency to default to structural causes alone by showing how immediate communication interacts with those structures.

remediation.action: Introduce a short historian debate excerpt (two historians with different views on print's role). Have students annotate which historian uses which kinds of evidence (circulation figures, reader responses, government reactions) and then ask students to design what additional evidence would strengthen each claim.
remediation.rationale: Exposing students to competing historical interpretations models the historian's method and emphasizes that claims rest on evidence (not just ideology). Asking for what would strengthen each side teaches students to look for concrete signs of causation (e.g., rapid spread of slogans, repression of presses) rather than assuming neutrality.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: Yes — because women were active in political life and formed clubs, the constitutions gave them voting and office rights.
diagnostic_questions.question: Did the 1791 and 1793 French constitutions grant women the right to vote and hold public office?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If a student answers 'yes', they are treating early activist visibility as equivalent to formal legal rights and failing to track legal change across the Revolution.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: No — women's clubs kept meeting and nothing legally stopped them, since women were clearly part of revolutionary politics.
diagnostic_questions.question: Was the existence of organised women's political clubs legally protected throughout the Revolution, including after 1793?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If a student answers 'no ban, they continued,' it shows they assume participation = continued inclusion and haven't noticed the October 1793 decree that outlawed women's clubs.

evidence.quote: Deprived of political rights by the Ancien Régime , the Revolution initially allowed women to participate, although only to a limited degree.
Despite this, the 1791 and 1793 constitutions denied them political rights and democratic citizenship.
the male-dominated Jacobins who then controlled the government denounced the Society as dangerous rabble-rousers and made all women's clubs and associations illegal.

learning_gaps.misconception: Women had equal political rights and full inclusion throughout the French Revolution.

remediation.action: Document jigsaw: give small groups short, labeled primary-source extracts (Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen 1789, article excerpts from the 1791 Constitution, relevant articles from the 1793 Constitution, and the October 1793 decree banning women's clubs). Each group reads its extract, summarises what political rights (if any) it promises and for whom, then students re-form mixed groups to compare summaries and produce a one-sentence timeline statement about legal rights for women at each date.
remediation.rationale: Exposure to the actual texts forces students to distinguish visible activism from legal status and to see the changing legal record across time. The jigsaw structure requires them to combine partial evidence rather than rely on a memorable episode, addressing the overgeneralisation from early activism.

remediation.action: Evidence timeline activity: provide mixed primary and secondary sources (pamphlets by women, contemporary newspaper reports of the March on Versailles, lists of women's societies, plus the 1791/1793 constitutional texts and the October 1793 police/jacobin decree). Students place each item on a classroom timeline and annotate whether it shows participation, legal recognition, or repression, then write a one-paragraph explanation of how women's political status changed over time citing at least two pieces of evidence.
remediation.rationale: Physically mapping events and documents highlights change over time and makes contradictions visible (high participation at certain moments vs later legal exclusion). Requiring citation trains students to ground claims in evidence and to resist sweeping statements based on a single dramatic example.

remediation.action: Perspective and causation discussion: present two short sources side-by-side — a letter or pamphlet by a female activist describing participation and demands, and the October 1793 decree or a Jacobin speech explaining the ban on women's clubs. Ask students in pairs to produce two brief arguments: (A) why revolutionaries supported women's inclusion early on; (B) why leaders later suppressed women’s organisations. Then hold a class debate weighing competing interpretations, asking students to cite the documents and to consider context (war, internal dissent, fears of factionalism).
remediation.rationale: This activity addresses both perspective and causation: students must account for why early inclusion did not guarantee continued rights and must evaluate competing historical explanations. It reinforces that the Revolution's policies changed in response to political context, not because women's activism always translated into formal equality.

periods.sequence_rationale: This opening period establishes the standard start/end dates and an evidence-based overview of the Revolution's long- and short-term causes. It prepares students to evaluate primary events next (Estates-General and National Assembly; Storming of the Bastille; Abolition of feudalism and August Decrees).
periods.title: What was the French Revolution? Definition & Causes

periods.sequence_rationale: This period builds on the prior overview of the Revolution's definition and causes by explaining how the Estates‑General crisis (May–June 1789) and the popular violence at the Bastille (14 July 1789) forced the National Assembly into radical action; it prepares students to evaluate the Assembly's later reforms such as the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and the fall of the monarchy.
periods.title: From Estates‑General to August Decrees

periods.sequence_rationale: This period builds on the Estates‑General, Bastille, and August Decrees by showing how the Revolution shifted into a constitutional monarchy and then collapsed after the Flight to Varennes; it prepares students to analyse the Republic's proclamation and Louis XVI's trial next.
periods.title: From Constitutional Monarchy to Republic Crisis

periods.sequence_rationale: This period builds on the fall of the monarchy and the controversies of the Constitutional Monarchy period taught in 'From Constitutional Monarchy to Republic Crisis' by explaining how the Convention proclaimed the Republic, tried and executed Louis XVI, and created the Committee of Public Safety. Understanding these events makes possible a study of the government and violence that follow in 'Reign of Terror (Sept 1793 – July 1794), Thermidorian Reaction and the Directory, Coup of 18 Brumaire and the Consulate'.
periods.title: From Republic Proclamation to Louis's Execution

periods.sequence_rationale: This period builds on the Republic proclamation, Louis XVI's trial and the Committee of Public Safety by examining how the Reign of Terror produced political instability; it prepares students to evaluate the Fall and execution of Robespierre, the Thermidorian reaction, and how that instability led to the Directory and ultimately the Coup of 18 Brumaire and the Consulate.
periods.title: Reign of Terror to 18 Brumaire

periods.sequence_rationale: This period takes students from the Reign of Terror’s end (the fall and execution of Robespierre and the repeal of the Law of 22 Prairial) toward the new constitutional order established by the Constitution of Year III and the Directory, preparing them to evaluate how the Thermidorian reaction shaped later military, political and economic developments under the Directory.
periods.title: Thermidor, Law of 22 Prairial, Directory

periods.sequence_rationale: This period builds on the fall of Robespierre, the end of the Terror and the Constitution of Year III (Thermidor, Law of 22 Prairial, Directory) by examining how the Directory governed amid war, press activity, and abolition; it prepares students to analyse Revolutionary symbols and economic crises in the following lesson (La Marseillaise; guillotine; symbols; role of women; assignats and inflation).
periods.title: Directory, Wars, and Colonial Emancipation

periods.sequence_rationale: This period builds on the prior study of newspapers, mobilisation and the Directory's political and economic challenges (Directory, Wars, and Colonial Emancipation) by tracing how songs, symbols and the guillotine shaped public opinion and how assignats and price controls produced popular hardship. It prepares students to evaluate the Revolution's long-term effects and to study the guillotine and assignats in greater depth in the following unit (Long-term impact of the Revolution on France and Europe; Guillotine; Assignats).
periods.title: Symbols, Terror, and Economic Crisis

periods.sequence_rationale: This period builds directly on 'Symbols, Terror, and Economic Crisis'—using the prior lesson's focus on La Marseillaise, the guillotine, the cockade, and assignats to move from events to interpretation. It prepares students to synthesize the Revolution's long-term impacts on France and Europe and to evaluate historiography through the bibliography and competing scholarly views.
periods.title: Revolutionary Symbols, Sources, and Legacy

Long-term impact of the Revolution on France and Europe: The Revolution ended feudalism in France, promoted individual freedoms, stimulated nationalism, exported reforms across Europe (notably Napoleonic legal codes), and influenced constitutions and reforms in several countries.
Estates-General: A representative body that last met in 1614 and was summoned to resolve fiscal crisis; its 1789 convening led to debates over voting by estate vs by head.
Assignats: Paper currency backed by nationalised church and émigr�e9 lands used during the Revolution; excessive issuance contributed to hyperinflation.

differentiation.extension: Design and describe a quantitative test using only classroom items here to compare the magnitude of charge transferred when rubbing the balloon vs rubbing the comb. Explain what measurable quantity you would use (for example, number of foil leaves separated, angle of deflection estimated visually) and how you would keep units or comparisons explicit (e.g., deflection distance in centimeters or count of attracted foil pieces). Predict the ratio of charges and explain the reasoning from electron transfer at the atomic scale.
differentiation.support: If you are unsure how to start, follow this worked example sentence: “I rubbed B with wool. B now attracts small pieces of foil; A does not. That means B gained electrons (more negative) and A lost none. I touched B to the key, then key to free foil three times, then key to taped foil three times. Both foils behaved the same, so total charge did not increase.” Pair a student who is unsure with a student who finished the first rub test.

materials: 2 balloons (one per pair)
small wool or cotton cloth (one per pair)
plastic comb or plastic pen (one per pair)
small metal key or paperclip (one per pair)
two 10 cm squares of aluminum foil (one pair share)
piece of sticky tape
marker
worksheet slip (teacher-printed, one per pair) — optional
student_instructions: 1. Label your two balloons or two objects A and B with the marker. Keep A untouched. Rub B with the wool cloth for 30 seconds. Observe whether A or B attracts the foil pieces, the comb, or the metal key.

2. Using the comb: rub the comb with the wool cloth for 15 seconds. Hold the comb near the two foil squares (not touching) and watch whether the foil squares move. Then hold the rubbed key or paperclip near each foil square. Record which object attracts or repels each foil square.

3. Redistribute charge test: Tape one aluminum foil square to the table and leave the other free. Touch the rubbed object (B or the comb) to the metal key, then touch that key to the free foil square three times. Next touch the key to the taped foil square three times. Observe whether the two foil pieces show the same behavior (both attracted to the comb or both repelled). Record whether the total visible effect on both foils changed after redistribution.

4. On your worksheet slip write: (a) which object gained electrons (felt negative), (b) which lost electrons (felt positive), (c) whether the two-foil system gained or lost net charge after your redistributions, and (d) one sentence: how this supports or opposes the idea that rubbing creates new charge.
success_criteria: Each pair has labeled their two test objects A and B and performed both a rubbing and a comb test (visible rubbed object and untouched object).
Each pair uses the metal key and the two foil squares to demonstrate charge transfer steps (touch sequences) and can point to whether both foil squares show the same sign after redistribution.
At least one member of each pair can state aloud which object gained electrons and which lost electrons, and that the two-foil system did not show a new extra net charge after redistribution.
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in pairs. Give each pair the listed materials. Say: “We will rub objects and watch where charges move. Our goal: show whether rubbing creates net charge or only moves electrons between materials.” Start a visible 12-minute timer.

2. Tell students to follow the student instructions. While they work, move between pairs. For the first 6 minutes watch that each pair performs the two rub tests in order (balloon–wool and comb–wool) and that they label which object was rubbed and which was not. Do not answer interpretive questions; instead ask, “What did you observe? Which object moved electrons according to your test?”

3. After 6 minutes give the prompt: “Now test whether the total charge in your two-object system changed. Use the foil pieces as charge indicators and your metal key to redistribute charge.” Observe for 4 minutes as pairs follow the redistribution step. If a pair stops, ask them to show how they are checking for net charge using the foil pieces.

4. In the last 2 minutes ask every pair to hold up both foil pieces and say aloud: “Do we find net charge left on the two-foil system after rubbing and redistribution? Yes or No — why?” Collect one quick sentence from 3–4 pairs to share with the class.

Show units and every algebraic step. Then explain qualitatively how the force on a small test charge +1.0×10^-9 C placed at the midpoint would compare to the force on q1 found earlier.

Pair with a neighbor who completed Part A for help on unit conversion.
