ruler (cm/mm)
worksheet (one per student) — printed problems below
periodic table or reference for electron charge value (optional)
student_instructions: Part A — Charge quantisation (4 minutes). A rubber rod is rubbed with fur and ends up with net charge +3.2 × 10^-18 C. Using the electron charge magnitude e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C, answer: (a) Calculate the integer n for the rod, where q = n·e. Show every step and include units. (b) Explain in one sentence whether rubbing created new charge or moved electrons between objects, using your n result as evidence.

Part B — Magnitude form of Coulomb's law (3 minutes). Two point charges are fixed on a lab bench: q1 = +4.8 × 10^-19 C (on the rod) and q2 = -3.2 × 10^-19 C (on a glass rod). They are separated by 5.0 cm. (a) Using Coulomb’s magnitude law F = k·|q1·q2|/r^2 with k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2, compute the magnitude of the force in newtons. Show units at each step and convert 5.0 cm to meters before substituting. (b) State whether the force is attraction or repulsion, and justify using the signs of q1 and q2.

Part C — Vector form direction (3 minutes). Place q1 at x = 0 m and q2 at x = +0.05 m on the x-axis. Using the vector form F_12 = k·q1·q2·(r_hat)/r^2 where r_hat points from charge 1 to charge 2, determine the force vector on q1 due to q2. (a) Compute the scalar value (including sign) that multiplies r_hat. (b) Give the final force as a vector in unit-vector notation (i.e., ±F î) with units.
Finish: Check that all numerical answers include units, that n in Part A is an integer, and that you showed the conversion between cm and m in Part B.
success_criteria: You can observe students writing q = n·e and calculating n as an integer (e.g., n = +20) with units C canceling correctly.
You can observe students converting 5.0 cm to 0.050 m before substituting into Coulomb's law and writing the force in newtons (e.g., 1.0 × 10^-8 N).

You can observe students indicating attraction or repulsion by citing the opposite or same signs of q1 and q2 and writing the force vector with the correct sign on the x-component (e.g., −Fx î for attraction toward +x).
teacher_instructions: 1. Hand out the worksheet (student_instructions below) and ask students to work individually. Say: “You have 10 minutes to complete all parts; show units and every algebraic step.” Start the timer.

2. While students work, circulate. For any student stuck at the start, point to the support box on their worksheet and read the first sentence frame aloud once. For students using wrong units, prompt: “What are the SI units for charge, distance, and force?”
3. After 8 minutes, announce: “Two minutes left — check that every step shows units and integer n when you use q = n·e.” Continue circulating to note observations listed under success_criteria.
4. At 10 minutes, collect worksheets and make quick notes on common errors (units, non-integer n, sign mistakes) to address in the next whole-class review.
activities.title: Counting Electrons and Calculating Coulomb Forces

differentiation.extension: For early finishers: change q1 to +5.0 μC at x = 0.00 m and q2 to +3.0 μC at x = 0.50 m. Calculate the electric field along the x-axis at x = 1.00 m (show all steps and units) and then compute the flux through a square area 0.050 m by 0.050 m placed at x = 1.00 m perpendicular to the x-axis if the local field is the field you computed. Explain how the sign of each charge affects the direction of the field contributions.
differentiation.support: If you are stuck, use this worked first item: For one point charge q = +1.0 μC at the origin, the field at r = 0.20 m on the +x axis is E = k*q/r^2 = (8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2)*(1.0×10^-6 C)/(0.20 m)^2 = 224.8×10^3 N/C ≈ 2.25×10^5 N/C directed in +x. Sentence frame for sketches: 'Field lines leave the positive charge and point ______ (toward/away) from it; at point P the field vector points ______.' If arithmetic is the barrier, pair with a student who can use the calculator while you label directions and units.

materials: 2 balloons (inflated)
wool cloth or sweater
2 lightweight foam or paper balls each tied to a ~30 cm thread (pith-ball substitute) or two small styrofoam balls on strings
marker and whiteboard or chart paper
ruler (30 cm)
calculator (class set or teacher-held)
printed worksheet with three short prompts (one per pair) — teacher can prepare in 5 minutes
student_instructions: 1) Watch the teacher demonstration closely and note whether the two rubbed balloons attract or repel, and how the foam pith-ball responds.

2) On your worksheet Part A: Draw field-line sketches for (i) a single positive point charge and (ii) a positive +3.0 μC and a negative −2.0 μC separated by 0.50 m. Show direction of field vectors at point P located midway (x = 0.25 m). Label arrows with 'E' and directions.

3) Part B (numeric superposition): Use Coulomb's law k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2. Compute magnitude and direction of E at P from q1 = +3.0 μC (at x = 0.00 m) and q2 = −2.0 μC (at x = 0.50 m). Show each step with units, then add vectorially to get net E at P in N/C. Write each r in meters and each intermediate result with units.
4) Part C (flux): Using E = 2000 N/C and area ΔS = 0.020 m^2 tilted at θ = 30°, compute the electric flux Φ through ΔS using Φ = E ΔS cosθ. Show units for Φ (N·m^2/C).
5) Hand your worksheet to the teacher when finished or raise your hand if you need help with any arithmetic step.
success_criteria: Each pair has a field-line sketch showing lines leaving the positive charge and ending on the negative charge, and a direction arrow for E at point P.
On at least four worksheets the teacher sees the step-by-step Coulomb calculations with numbers and units for E1 and E2 and a correct vector sum (net E in N/C).
Most pairs have a written value for flux Φ with correct substitution Φ = E ΔS cosθ and units N·m^2/C.
teacher_instructions: 1) Grouping and setup (1 minute): Arrange students in pairs. Ask each pair to watch the demonstration and to complete the short worksheet supplied: (A) sketch field lines, (B) answer a numeric superposition question, (C) compute a simple flux. Hand one worksheet to each pair.

2) Demonstration start (2 minutes): At the front, rub both balloons briskly with the wool cloth for 15–20 seconds. Hold the two balloons near each other on strings so students can see whether they attract or repel. Also approach a pith-ball substitute (foam ball on string) to show attraction/repulsion. Say aloud: “We will use this to reason about electron transfer and how fields combine.”

3) Explain atomic-scale charge transfer (2 minutes): While students watch the balloons, draw two neutral atoms on the board. Show, step by step, electrons moving from one material to another when rubbed (label electrons with charge −e, units coulomb C). Say: “Electrons move; protons stay in the nuclei. Rubbing transfers electrons so one object gains a net negative charge and the other loses electrons and is net positive. The total net charge of the pair equals the difference of electrons moved — electrons are conserved in transfer.”

4) Superposition demonstration and quick calculation (3 minutes): Place two point-charge symbols on the board: q1 = +3.0 μC at x = 0.00 m and q2 = −2.0 μC at x = 0.50 m. Tell students you will compute electric field at P at x = 0.25 m. Write Coulomb's law E = k*q/r^2 (show units N/C) and compute E1 from q1 and E2 from q2 with numeric values, carrying units: k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2. Show vector directions, add them to get net E (show step-by-step numbers and final N/C).

5) Field lines and flux explanation (2 minutes): Ask pairs to sketch field lines around a positive and negative charge on their worksheet, emphasizing lines leaving positive and ending on negative and greater density = stronger field. Then demonstrate flux: draw a small area element ΔS = 0.020 m^2 at angle θ = 30° to a uniform E = 2000 N/C and compute Φ = E·ΔS = E ΔS cosθ, showing units (N·m^2/C). Ask students to finish their worksheet in the remaining minute.
activities.title: Balloon Charge Demo, Field Sketch, and Quick Superposition Calculation

differentiation.extension: Derive the far-field electric field at an arbitrary point specified by vector r (not on the axis) to show the full angular dependence E(r) ≈ (1/4πε0)(1/r^3)(3(p·r̂) r̂ - p). Start from the two-charge vector sum, carry out a series expansion for r >> a to first order in a/r, and show each vector algebra step, with units carried through. Then compute a numerical example for p along +x and a field point at polar angle θ = 60° and r = 1.0 m using q = 1.0×10^-6 C and a = 0.01 m.
differentiation.support: If you are stuck, copy this starting work: E_x(r) = (1/4πε0) q [ 1/(r - a)^2 - 1/(r + a)^2 ]. Then form a common denominator: 1/(r - a)^2 - 1/(r + a)^2 = ((r + a)^2 - (r - a)^2) / ((r - a)^2 (r + a)^2). Expand the numerator: (r^2 + 2ar + a^2) - (r^2 - 2ar + a^2) = 4ar. So E_x(r) = (1/4πε0) q (4ar) / ((r - a)^2 (r + a)^2). For r >> a, approximate (r - a)^2 (r + a)^2 ≈ r^4; then E_x ≈ (1/4πε0) q (4a r) / r^4 = (1/4πε0) (4qa / r^3). Recall p = q·(2a), so this gives E_x ≈ (1/4πε0)(2p / r^3).

materials: whiteboard or chalkboard
calculator (one per student or pair)
ruler or straightedge
graph paper or plain paper
pen or pencil
stopwatch or classroom clock
textbook or formula sheet (optional)
student_instructions: 1. Work in pairs. One person writes algebra; the other does arithmetic. We place +q at x = +a and −q at x = −a along the x-axis. Use q = symbol q (keep q general) and a = symbol a (keep a general) for the derivation. Use SI units (q in coulombs, a in metres, r in metres).

2. Write the electric field at a point on the +x axis at position x = r as the vector sum of the fields from each charge. For the +q at x = +a, the field at x = r is E_+ = (1/4πε0) q (r - a)̂ / (r - a)^2. For the −q at x = −a, the field at x = r is E_- = (1/4πε0)(-q) (r + a)̂ / (r + a)^2. Show the direction signs explicitly so you have scalar x-components:
- E_+,_x = (1/4πε0) * q / (r - a)^2 (directed +x if r > a)
- E_- ,_x = (1/4πε0) * ( - q ) / (r + a)^2 (directed +x because negative charge pulls toward −a).

3. Sum the x-components: E_x(r) = (1/4πε0) q [ 1/(r - a)^2 - 1/(r + a)^2 ]. Put over a common denominator and simplify algebraically. Show each algebra step. Replace q·(2a) by p when you reach that product and state p's units (C·m).

4. Assume r >> a. Use the binomial approximation: 1/(r ± a)^2 ≈ 1/r^2 * (1 ∓ 2a/r). Show the simplification step-by-step and keep units. Derive E_x ≈ (1/4πε0) (2q·(2a) / r^3) / 2 if needed and reduce to the canonical form E_axis = (1/4πε0)(2p / r^3). Write p = q·(2a) and verify units: E in N/C.

5. Numerical check: using q = 1.0×10^-6 C and a = 0.01 m, compute exact E_x at r = 0.5 m by summing the two Coulomb contributions with distances (r - a) and (r + a). Then compute the far-field approximation E_axis_approx = (1/4πε0)(2p / r^3) for the same r. Repeat at r = 1.0 m. Compare the ratios Exact/Approx and show whether they approach 1 as r increases. Record your arithmetic and units for each step.
success_criteria: At least one pair has algebra written showing the two scalar x-component terms 1/(r - a)^2 and 1/(r + a)^2 and their subtraction.
Pairs carry out the binomial approximation explicitly on paper (showing 1/(r ± a)^2 ≈ 1/r^2 (1 ∓ 2a/r)) and write the resulting 1/r^3 dependence with p = q·(2a) and units indicated.

Pairs have numeric work visible for r = 0.5 m and r = 1.0 m showing exact sum and approximate value and a reported ratio Exact/Approx (teacher can read one pair’s ratio to confirm values are converging toward 1).
teacher_instructions: 1. Group students in pairs. Say: “You will derive the far-field electric field of a simple dipole (+q and −q separated by 2a) and then check the 1/r^3 dependence numerically. Work with your partner; one writes and one calculates.” Start the stopwatch for 12 minutes and announce time checkpoints at 7 minutes and 2 minutes remaining.

2. On the board, draw the dipole on the x-axis: +q at x = +a and −q at x = −a. Write Coulomb's law vector form for a point charge at the origin: E(r) = (1/4πε0) Q r̂ / r^2. Tell students they will place the field point on the +x axis at coordinate x = r (r >> a).

3. Tell students to derive the expression for the x-component of the total field on the axis by summing the two contributions using vector form, then expand for r >> a using the binomial approximation. Circulate while pairs work, watching for correct substitution of position vectors, consistent units (meters, coulombs, N/C), and explicit steps in the binomial expansion. If a pair is stuck, point them to the support scaffold on the worksheet (read it aloud if needed).

4. After 7 minutes, call the class back together for a 2-minute comparison: ask one pair to write the derived far-field expression in terms of dipole moment p = q(2a) or p = q·(2a) on the board and to state the units of p and of E. Confirm the axis result E_axis = (1/4πε0)(2p / r^3) and identify units (p in C·m, E in N/C).

5. Return students to pairs for the remaining time to compute numerical values: give q = 1.0×10^-6 C and a = 0.01 m. Have them compute E at r = 0.5 m and r = 1.0 m using both exact Coulomb sums and the far-field approximation; then compare the ratio to check ~1/r^3 scaling. Collect one completed example from any pair or call on a pair to report their numerical ratio at the end.
activities.title: Dipole Far-Field Derivation and r^-3 Check

differentiation.extension: If finished early: (a) Recompute the net force on q3 if q2 is moved to x = 0.40 m. Show how the signs and magnitudes change and explain physically why. (b) For the flux item, compute the flux through a patch whose area vector makes 60° with E_net and compare magnitudes. (c) For the dipole, write the full vector torque τ (use unit vector notation) when p points at 30° above +y in the xy-plane and E = 2.0×10^5 N/C in +y.
differentiation.support: If you are stuck: (a) Start by computing the two distances to q3: r13 = 0.50 m and r23 = 0.20 m. (b) Compute one Coulomb force first: F_13 = k * q1 * q3 / r13^2; sign: q1 and q3 are both positive so force on q3 from q1 is +x (repulsive). Work that number out first, then compute F_23 and remember q2 is negative so it attracts q3 (direction -x). For the torque item, use the numerical form τ = p E sin(30°) = p E * 0.5 as the worked first step.

materials: whiteboard or chart paper
marker
calculator (optional)
printed one-page prompt per student (teacher can copy the student_instructions text)
student_instructions: Think phase (3 min, individual): Answer the three numbered tasks below. Show units and at least one short derivation step for each numeric result.

1) Superposition force (do the vector addition step): Three point charges lie on the x-axis: q1 = +2.0 μC at x = 0 m, q2 = -1.0 μC at x = 0.30 m, and q3 = +1.0 μC at x = 0.50 m. Find the net electrostatic force on q3. Use Coulomb's law F = k q_i q_j / r^2, with k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2. Show directions as +x or -x and carry units (N). Write the two forces on q3 from q1 and q2, then add them.

2) Small-area flux (one short dot product): At the location of q3, imagine a small flat square patch of area A = 1.0×10^-4 m^2 whose area vector points in the +x direction. Using the net electric field at q3 found by dividing your net force by q3 (E_net = F_net / q3), compute the electric flux through the patch: Φ = E_net · A = E_net * A * cosθ. State θ and units (V·m or N·m^2/C).

3) Densities and dipole torque (definitions and a quick torque calc): (a) Give the definition and SI unit for linear charge density λ, surface density σ, and volume density ρ, each in one short sentence (include symbol, formula relating a small element of charge dq, and unit). Example format: λ = dq/dl, unit C·m^-1. (b) A dipole with moment p = 4.0×10^-29 C·m is in a uniform electric field E = 2.0×10^5 N/C directed +y. Calculate the magnitude of the torque τ when the dipole is oriented at 30° from +y. Show the vector or magnitude step from τ = p × E and give units (N·m).
Pair phase (4 min): Compare your answers; if you disagreed, re-calculate the numeric steps together. Agree on one clear line-by-line solution to write down.
Share phase (3 min): Be ready to present your pair's solution for the part assigned by the teacher.
success_criteria: Circulating teacher can see each pair write the two individual Coulomb forces on q3 with signs (+x or -x) and numeric values in newtons before summing them.
Each pair computes E_net at q3 with units N/C and uses it to calculate flux Φ through the small patch, showing the angle θ used and the product E_net·A with units.
On the densities/torque item, each pair writes the three density definitions with correct units (C·m^-1, C·m^-2, C·m^-3) and shows the torque magnitude computed from τ = p E sinθ with units N·m.
teacher_instructions: 1. Hand each student a printed prompt (or project the student_instructions). Tell students: "You have 3 minutes to work silently and answer the three numbered items for yourself." Start a visible 3-minute timer.

2. After 3 minutes, ask students to pair up with a neighbor. Say: "You have 4 minutes to compare answers, agree on one written solution per pair, and write any corrected steps on your paper or the whiteboard." Circulate and listen for reasoning; when you hear an incorrect step, point them to re-check vector directions or units but do not give the answer.

3. After 4 minutes of pair work, call for two pairs to share their solutions on the board (1 pair for the force question, 1 pair for densities/flux/torque). Allow 3 minutes total for the two groups to present and for you to make one clear correction or highlight one correct derivation step.
activities.title: Three Charges, a Patch, and a Dipole: Quick Think-Pair-Share

differentiation.extension: Derive the electric field on the axis a distance z from the center of a finite uniformly charged disk of radius a and surface charge density σ by integrating concentric rings. Show units at every step and reduce your result to the plane limit (a → ∞) to recover E = σ/(2ε0).
differentiation.support: If you are stuck, start with this sentence frame and worked example for the wire: 'Choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r = ___ m and length L = 1.0 m. By symmetry E is constant on the curved surface and perpendicular to it. Gauss's law gives E(2πrL) = Q_enc/ε0. With linear charge density λ (C/m), Q_enc = λL (C). So E = λ/(2π ε0 r). For λ = 5.0×10⁻⁸ C/m and r = 0.20 m: E = (5.0×10⁻⁸ C/m) / [2π(8.85×10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²))(0.20 m)]. Carry units: C/m divided by (C²/(N·m²)·m) = N/C. Compute with your calculator to get a numeric N/C value.'

materials: chalkboard or whiteboard
markers or chalk
meter stick
calculator for each pair
one printed A4 slip per pair with numerical example values (see teacher_instructions)
student_instructions: Work with your partner. Read your printed slip and identify which of the three cases (wire, plane, spherical shell) you will solve numerically and which you must still derive symbolically.

Step 1 — Write Gauss's law in integral form: ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε0. Explain aloud which Gaussian surface you choose and why its symmetry makes E constant over the surface portion you use. State the surface and its dimensions and label all distances with units (e.g., r = 0.20 m).

Step 2 — Convert the surface integral into E times the appropriate area using symmetry. For each case show algebraic steps and include units: for the wire use a cylindrical surface of length L (m) and radius r (m) so ∮E·dA = E(2πrL) with units V/m × m² = N·m/C? (keep SI units and show cancellation to get N/C); for the plane use a pillbox of area A (m²) giving ∮E·dA = E(2A) etc.; for the shell show that Q_enc = q for r>R and Q_enc = 0 for r<R and use a spherical surface of area 4πr² (m²).

Step 3 — Rearrange to solve for E symbolically, showing ε0 with its units (ε0 = 8.85×10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²)). Write the final formula with units: wire E = λ/(2π ε0 r) (units N/C); plane E = σ/(2ε0) (units N/C); shell outside E = q/(4πε0 r²) (N/C) and shell inside E = 0 (N/C).

Step 4 — Substitute the numerical values from your slip into the derived formula, carry units through the arithmetic, compute a numeric value and include units N/C. Record one clear sentence describing the physical meaning of the result (for example: 'At r = 0.20 m from the wire the magnitude of the electric field is ... N/C radially outward').
success_criteria: Each pair has drawn and labeled the Gaussian surface (cylinder, pillbox, or sphere) with distances in metres visible on their paper or board.
Each pair writes Gauss's law ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε0 and shows the algebraic step where the surface integral becomes E times the area (e.g., E·2πrL for the cylinder) while including units.
Each pair computes a numeric value with units (N/C) on their paper for their assigned numerical example and can point to the step where units cancel to give N/C.
teacher_instructions: Arrange students in pairs. Hand each pair a printed slip with one numerical example: (A) λ = 5.0×10⁻⁸ C/m and r = 0.20 m for the wire; (B) σ = 2.0×10⁻⁶ C/m² for the infinite plane; (C) q = 6.0×10⁻⁶ C and R = 0.10 m for the spherical shell and ask them to compute both outside (r = 0.20 m) and inside (r = 0.05 m). Say: 'You have 10 minutes to derive each formula from Gauss's law, show units at each step, and compute the field numerically for your given example.'

Start a visible timer and announce time checkpoints at 6 minutes and 2 minutes remaining. While pairs work, circulate to check that each pair: (a) chooses an appropriate Gaussian surface, (b) writes Gauss's law in integral form ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε0, and (c) carries units through each algebraic step.

If a pair finishes early, direct them to the extension problem on their slip (derive the on-axis field for a finite uniformly charged disk at a point a distance z from the center) and provide a scrap sheet for extra derivation. If a pair is stuck after 3 minutes, offer the support scaffold (below) and prompt them to start with the worked first item.

After time is up, call for one pair to present the wire derivation, one pair the plane derivation, and one pair the spherical shell derivation; limit each presentation to 60 seconds and correct any missing unit or step on the board.
activities.title: Derive E for Wire, Plane, and Spherical Shell with Gauss's Law

items.answer: F_on_2 = (−0.129 N) i + (−0.173 N) j. Magnitude |F_on_2| = 0.216 N, directed from q2 toward q1 (along the vector −0.6 i −0.8 j).

rubric.criteria: Correct vector electrostatic force on q2 due to q1, with units and clear use of Coulomb's law.

levels.descriptor: All steps shown: charges converted to coulombs, displacement and distance computed correctly (r = 0.50 m), correct unit vector (−0.6, −0.8, 0), correct magnitude 0.216 N to three significant figures, and correct components Fx = −0.129 N, Fy = −0.173 N with units.
levels.label: Full credit

levels.descriptor: Most steps correct but with one of the following errors: correct magnitude but one component sign or direction incorrect; or correct components but magnitude not calculated/rounded properly; or units missing. Work must show Coulomb's law and use of r̂. Award 2 marks.
levels.label: Partial credit

levels.descriptor: Incorrect or no application of Coulomb's law, wrong distance or unit vector, or numerical result unrelated to shown working. No clear steps connecting Coulomb's law to a vector answer.
levels.label: No credit

items.stem: Two point charges are located in the xy-plane: charge q1 = +3.0 μC is at r1 = (0.00, 0.00, 0.00) m and charge q2 = −2.0 μC is at r2 = (0.30, 0.40, 0.00) m. Using Coulomb's law in vector form, calculate the electrostatic force (vector) on q2 due to q1. Give your answer in newtons with components Fx and Fy to three significant figures.
items.working:
Step 1 — Convert charges to coulombs: q1 = +3.0 μC = +3.0×10^−6 C, q2 = −2.0 μC = −2.0×10^−6 C.
Step 2 — Find displacement from q2 to q1: r = r1 − r2 = (0.00 − 0.30, 0.00 − 0.40, 0.00 − 0.00) m = (−0.30, −0.40, 0.00) m.
Step 3 — Compute separation distance r = √[ (−0.30)^2 + (−0.40)^2 ] m = √(0.09 + 0.16) m = √0.25 m = 0.50 m.
Step 4 — Unit vector from q2 toward q1: r̂ = r / r = (−0.30/0.50, −0.40/0.50, 0) = (−0.6, −0.8, 0).
Step 5 — Use Coulomb's constant k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2 and Coulomb's law in vector form:
F_on_2 = k q2 q1 / r^2 · r̂.
Compute q1 q2 = (3.0×10^−6 C)(−2.0×10^−6 C) = −6.0×10^−12 C^2.
Compute denominator r^2 = (0.50 m)^2 = 0.25 m^2.
Magnitude prefactor = k |q1 q2| / r^2 = (8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2)(6.0×10^−12 C^2) / 0.25 m^2 = (8.99×10^9)(2.4×10^−11) N = 0.21576 N.
The sign from q1 q2 is negative, indicating the force on q2 is toward q1, consistent with r̂ pointing toward q1. Thus vector force:
F_on_2 = (−0.21576 N) · r̂ = (−0.21576)(−0.6, −0.8, 0)?? (Note: the negative sign is already in q1 q2; applying correctly gives F = (−0.21576)·(−0.6, −0.8,0) would be positive — instead handle sign carefully below.)
Better: take magnitude 0.21576 N and direction r̂ (which already points from q2 to q1). Because q1 q2 is negative the force is along r̂ (toward q1). Therefore components:
Fx = 0.21576 × (−0.6) = −0.129456 N → −0.129 N (3 s.f.).
Fy = 0.21576 × (−0.8) = −0.172608 N → −0.173 N (3 s.f.).
Magnitude |F_on_2| = 0.21576 N → 0.216 N (3 s.f.).
Final answer: F_on_2 = (−0.129 N) i + (−0.173 N) j, magnitude 0.216 N directed from q2 toward q1.

items.answer: 0.75 N directed to the left (negative x-direction). Reason: F1 = k(1.0e-6)(2.0e-6)/(0.20^2) = 0.4495 N left; F2 = k(1.0e-6)(3.0e-6)/(0.30^2) = 0.2997 N left; net F = 0.4495 + 0.2997 = 0.7492 N ≈ 0.75 N, left.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Correct. Compute each force with Coulomb's law: F1 from q1: k(1.0e-6 C)(2.0e-6 C)/(0.20 m)^2 = 0.4495 N directed left (repulsion). F2 from q2: k(1.0e-6)(3.0e-6)/(0.30 m)^2 = 0.2997 N directed left (attraction). Vector sum = 0.4495 + 0.2997 = 0.7492 N ≈ 0.75 N left.
options.text: 0.75 N directed to the left (negative x-direction)

options.label: B
options.rationale: Incorrect direction. This option has the correct magnitude but the wrong sign. Both individual forces point to the left (q0 is repelled by +q1 to the left and attracted to −q2 to the left), so the net force cannot be to the right.
options.text: 0.75 N directed to the right (positive x-direction)

options.label: C

items.stem: A test charge q0 = +1.0 μC sits at the origin (x = 0). Two other point charges lie on the x-axis: q1 = +2.0 μC at x = +0.20 m and q2 = −3.0 μC at x = −0.30 m. Using Coulomb's constant k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2 and the principle of superposition, what is the net electrostatic force on q0 (give magnitude and direction along the x-axis)?

items.answer:
(a) Infinite straight wire (linear charge density λ): Choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L coaxial with the wire. By symmetry E is radial and constant on the curved surface; flux = E(2πrL). Enclosed charge = λL. Gauss's law: E(2πrL) = λL/ε0 ⇒ E = λ/(2π ε0 r), directed radially outward. Units: C m−1 / (ε0·m) = N C−1.

(b) Infinite plane (surface charge density σ): Choose a pillbox (cylinder) of area A penetrating the plane so it has two flat faces, one on each side. Field is normal and equal in magnitude on both sides, and negligible on the curved side. Flux = E·A + E·A = 2EA. Enclosed charge = σA. Gauss's law: 2EA = σA/ε0 ⇒ E = σ/(2ε0), directed normal to the plane (same magnitude on both sides). Units: C m−2/(ε0) = N C−1.

(c) Thin spherical shell (total charge q, radius R): Use a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius r.
- For r > R (outside): flux = E(4πr^2). Enclosed charge = q. Gauss's law: E(4πr^2) = q/ε0 ⇒ E = q/(4πε0 r^2), as if all charge were at the centre, radial outward. Units: C/(ε0·m^2) = N C−1.
- For r < R (inside): Gaussian surface encloses no charge (enclosed charge = 0 because shell is thin). Thus flux = E(4πr^2) = 0 ⇒ E = 0 inside the shell.

rubric.criteria: Correct use of Gauss's law and appropriate Gaussian surface to derive each requested electric field expression, with units and direction stated.

levels.descriptor: All three cases correctly derived: (a) cylindrical surface leading to E = λ/(2π ε0 r) with radial direction and units; (b) pillbox giving E = σ/(2ε0) with direction and units; (c) spherical surface giving E = q/(4πε0 r^2) for r>R and E = 0 for r<R, with units. Each derivation shows chosen Gaussian surface, flux = q_enc/ε0 step, and algebraic solution for E.
levels.label: Full credit

levels.descriptor: One or two cases correctly derived with appropriate Gaussian surface, flux equation, and solved expression (with units). Missing or incorrect derivation for the remaining case(s), or correct final formulas given without one clear flux/enclosed-charge step.
levels.label: Partial credit

levels.descriptor: No correct derivations; final expressions absent or incorrect for all three cases, or Gauss's law/flux steps not used at all.
levels.label: No credit

items.stem: Use Gauss's law to derive the magnitude of the electric field in each case. Show the Gaussian surface you choose, write the flux = enclosed charge/ε0 relation, and solve for E. (a) At distance r from an infinitely long straight wire with linear charge density λ. (b) Near an infinite uniformly charged plane with surface charge density σ. (c) Outside (r > R) and inside (r < R) a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of total charge q and radius R.
items.working:
(a) Wire:
1. Choose cylindrical Gaussian surface radius r, length L centered on wire.
2. By cylindrical symmetry E is radial and constant on curved surface; contributions on end caps are zero.
3. Electric flux Φ = ∮E·dA = E(2πrL).
4. Enclosed charge q_enc = λL.
5. Gauss's law: Φ = q_enc/ε0 ⇒ E(2πrL) = λL/ε0.
6. Solve: E = λ/(2π ε0 r). Units: λ (C m−1) divided by ε0 (C^2 N−1 m−2) and length r (m) yields N C−1.

(b) Infinite plane:
1. Choose pillbox crossing plane with flat faces area A; symmetry gives E normal and same magnitude on both sides.
2. Flux Φ = E·A (top) + E·A (bottom) = 2EA.
3. Enclosed charge q_enc = σA.
4. Gauss's law: 2EA = σA/ε0 ⇒ E = σ/(2ε0).
5. Direction: normal to plane, same magnitude on both sides. Units: σ (C m−2) over ε0 gives field in N C−1.

(c) Thin spherical shell:
1. Choose spherical Gaussian surface radius r concentric with shell.
2. By symmetry E is radial and constant on sphere: flux Φ = E(4πr^2).
3. If r > R: q_enc = q, so E(4πr^2) = q/ε0 ⇒ E = q/(4πε0 r^2).
4. If r < R: q_enc = 0 (no charge enclosed inside shell), so E(4πr^2) = 0 ⇒ E = 0.
5. Units: q (C) divided by ε0 (C^2 N−1 m−2) and r^2 (m^2) yields N C−1.

items.answer: Rubbing brings surfaces into close contact so that electrons can move from atoms on one surface to atoms on the other. Which way electrons move depends on the relative tendency of the materials’ surface atoms to hold electrons (electron affinity or work function). For example, plastic tends to gain electrons from hair, so individual electrons (each with charge −e where e = 1.602×10^−19 C) move from hair atoms to the comb. Each electron removed from the hair leaves behind a positive ion (a deficit of one electron) and each electron gained by the comb produces an extra negative charge. Because charge is quantised, every transferred amount is an integer multiple of e: q_transferred = n·e for some integer n (n is the number of electrons moved). Conservation of charge requires that the total charge of the isolated two-object system does not change during contact and rubbing: every electron that leaves the hair appears on the comb, so the negative charge gained by the comb equals in magnitude the positive charge left on the hair. Thus rubbing redistributes charge between the two bodies but does not create net charge; the sum of their charges before and after rubbing is the same. As an illustrative number: if 10^12 electrons transfer, the comb gains −n e = −(10^12)(1.602×10^−19 C) = −1.60×10^−7 C and the hair gains +1.60×10^−7 C, leaving the total unchanged.

rubric.criteria: Explanation combining atomic-scale electron transfer, conservation of charge, and quantisation (with an example or numerical illustration).

levels.descriptor: Explains that rubbing allows electrons to move between surface atoms (states reason: electron affinity/work function difference), states that each transferred particle is an electron of charge −e and that transferred charge is q = n·e, and explicitly applies conservation of charge to show the negative charge gained by one object equals the positive charge left on the other; includes a correct numerical illustration using e = 1.602×10^−19 C or an equivalent integer-multiple statement. All key points correct and clearly connected.
levels.label: Full credit

levels.descriptor: Identifies that electrons move from one object to the other and mentions either conservation of charge or quantisation but not both fully; gives a correct qualitative account that charge is redistributed (not created) but lacks a clear integer/electron explanation or a numerical/quantisation statement, or contains a minor omission or small inaccuracy in connecting the principles.
levels.label: Partial credit

levels.descriptor: Gives an incorrect or very incomplete explanation (e.g. states rubbing 'creates charge' or only describes macroscopic observation without atomic mechanism), does not mention conservation or quantisation, or contains fundamental errors about where charge comes from.
levels.label: Minimal / no credit

items.stem: When you rub a plastic comb on dry hair the comb becomes negatively charged and the hair becomes positively charged. Using an atomic-scale description of charge transfer, explain why rubbing transfers electrons between the two objects but does not create or destroy net electric charge. In your answer include how the conservation and quantisation of charge apply to this process. (6 marks)

items.answer:
(a) On the positive z-axis (θ = 0): E = (1/4πε0) (2 p / r^3) ẑ.

(b) On the equatorial plane (θ = 90°): E = −(1/4πε0) (p / r^3) ẑ.

rubric.criteria: Correct derivation and expression of the dipole far-field on axis and on the equatorial plane in terms of p, using r >> a approximations.

levels.descriptor: Both (a) and (b) derived correctly with clear superposition, appropriate approximations for r >> a, correct algebraic simplification to E = (1/4πε0)(2p/r^3) ẑ on-axis and E = −(1/4πε0)(p/r^3) ẑ on the equator, and units/factors 1/(4πε0) shown.
levels.label: Full marks

levels.descriptor: One of the two positions (either axis or equator) derived correctly with correct use of p and approximations, or both derived but with a minor algebraic slip that does not change dependence on p and r (e.g. a factor-of-2 error on one step but final expressions show correct 1/r^3 scaling and correct sign for at least one case).
levels.label: Partial credit

items.stem: A simple electric dipole consists of two point charges +q and −q placed on the z-axis at z = +a and z = −a respectively. Let p denote the dipole moment vector p = 2a q ẑ (pointing from −q to +q). Assuming the field point is at distance r from the origin with r >> a, (a) derive the far-field electric field on the positive z-axis (θ = 0) and express it in terms of p; (b) derive the far-field electric field at a point on the equatorial plane (θ = 90°) at distance r from the origin and express it in terms of p. Give your answers in SI units and keep factors of 1/(4πε0) explicit. (Total 4 marks)
items.working:
(a) On-axis (point at z = r, r >> a):
- Electric field is superposition of fields from +q at z = +a and −q at z = −a, both along ẑ.
- Field from +q at distance r−a: E+ = (1/4πε0) q / (r−a)^2 in +ẑ direction.
- Field from −q at distance r+a: E− = (1/4πε0) (−q) / (r+a)^2 in +ẑ direction (because −q produces field toward it).
- Net E_z = (1/4πε0) [ q/(r−a)^2 − q/(r+a)^2 ]
- Expand for r >> a using binomial approximation: 1/(r∓a)^2 ≈ 1/r^2 (1 ± 2a/r + ...).
  So q[(1/(r−a)^2) − (1/(r+a)^2)] ≈ q[ (1/r^2)(1+2a/r) − (1/r^2)(1−2a/r) ] = q(4a / r^3).
- Thus E_z ≈ (1/4πε0) (4 a q / r^3) = (1/4πε0) (2 p / r^3) since p = 2 a q. Direction is +ẑ.

(b) Equatorial plane (point at x = r, z = 0, r >> a):
- Consider vertical (z) components; horizontal components from +q and −q cancel by symmetry.
- Field from +q located at z = +a: its z-component is E+_z = (1/4πε0) q [−a] / (r^2 + a^2)^{3/2} (negative because it points toward +q, i.e. downward).
- Field from −q at z = −a: its z-component is E−_z = (1/4πε0) (−q) [+a] / (r^2 + a^2)^{3/2} (also negative contribution).
- Net E_z = (1/4πε0) [ q(−a) − q( a) ] / (r^2 + a^2)^{3/2} = (1/4πε0) [ −2 q a ] / (r^2 + a^2)^{3/2}.
- For r >> a, (r^2 + a^2)^{3/2} ≈ r^3, so E_z ≈ −(1/4πε0) (2 q a / r^3) = −(1/4πε0) (p / r^3).
- Direction is −ẑ (toward the negative z-direction).

items.answer: λ is charge per unit length (C/m), σ is charge per unit area (C/m^2), ρ is charge per unit volume (C/m^3). Reasoning: by definition a linear charge distribution gives charge Q over a small length dl so λ = dQ/dl (units C/m), a surface distribution gives dQ/dA so σ = dQ/dA (C/m^2), and a volume distribution gives dQ/dV so ρ = dQ/dV (C/m^3).

options.label: A

options.label: D

items.stem: Which of the following gives the correct definitions and SI units for the linear, surface, and volume charge densities (λ, σ, ρ)?

items.answer: Operational definition: Place a small positive test charge q0 at the point and measure the electrostatic force F experienced by that test charge. The electric field vector at that point is defined as E = F / q0 (so E points in the direction of the force on a positive test charge). The SI unit of E is newtons per coulomb (N C^-1). As an example, the field of a point charge Q at the origin is E(r) = (1 / 4πε0) · Q r̂ / r^2, in N C^-1.

rubric.criteria: Correct operational definition (procedure and equation), statement of direction, and correct SI unit

levels.descriptor: Clearly states the measurement procedure (place small positive test charge q0 and measure force F), gives the correct relation E = F/q0 with E as a vector and notes that E points in the direction of the force on a positive test charge, and states the SI unit N C^-1 (or N/C). May include the point-charge example formula.
levels.label: Full marks

levels.descriptor: Gives the correct formula E = F/q0 and the SI unit N C^-1 but omits either the explicit measurement procedure (placing a test charge) or the statement about the direction of E for a positive test charge, or presents these parts ambiguously.
levels.label: Partial credit

items.stem: Give the operational definition of the electric field at a point in space. In your answer, state how you would measure it with a test charge, provide the formula that relates the measured quantity to the electric field (use symbols), and give the SI unit of the electric field. (3 marks)

items.answer:
Inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium the electric field is zero because free charges within the conductor move until there is no net force on them. If any electric field existed in the conducting material, free electrons (or positive charges) would feel a force and move, contradicting equilibrium. To show this using Gauss's law, choose a Gaussian surface entirely inside the conducting material (but within the metal, not in the cavity). Because charges in a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium reside only on surfaces, the net charge enclosed by this Gaussian surface is zero. Gauss's law, ∮E·dA = Q_enclosed/ε0, then gives ∮E·dA = 0, and by symmetry and continuity of E in the metal this implies E = 0 everywhere inside the conductor.

Because the field inside the conducting material is zero, any excess free charge placed on the conductor must move to locations where it can produce no internal field in the metal: those are the conductor surfaces. Therefore excess charge resides on the outer surface of the hollow sphere.

If a point charge is placed inside the cavity (not touching the conductor), the free charges in the conductor rearrange: an induced charge equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to the point charge appears on the inner cavity surface so that the field inside the conductor material remains zero. The conductor as a whole may also acquire an additional charge on its outer surface: the total charge on the outer surface equals the original excess charge placed on the conductor plus any charge on the conductor before insertion, minus the induced inner-surface charge. For an isolated neutral conducting shell with a +q point charge in the cavity, an induced −q appears on the inner surface and +q appears on the outer surface. Outside the sphere (for a spherical conductor) the field is as if all net charge were concentrated at the centre — for a general shaped conductor the external field depends only on the net charge on the conductor and not on the position of the charge inside the cavity. The induced inner charge ensures the conductor material has zero internal field, satisfying electrostatic equilibrium and Gauss's law.

rubric.criteria: Correct use of Gauss's law and electrostatic equilibrium to explain zero internal field, surface charge location, and induced charges when a cavity contains a point charge.

levels.descriptor: Shows that any internal E would move free charges and so cannot exist; selects a Gaussian surface inside the conductor, states Q_enclosed = 0 and applies Gauss's law to conclude E = 0 in the metal. Clearly explains that excess charge must therefore be on the outer surface. Describes induced −q on the inner cavity surface when a point charge +q is placed in the cavity (and corresponding +q on the outer surface for an initially neutral shell), and states how the external field depends only on the net charge (for a sphere it is as if charge at the centre).
levels.label: Excellent (6 marks)

levels.descriptor: States that the electric field inside a conductor is zero and that excess charge resides on the surface, but provides only a qualitative argument without correctly using Gauss's law, or gives an incomplete description of induced charges (e.g. mentions induction but fails to state the equal-and-opposite induced inner charge or its effect on outer charge).
levels.label: Partial (3 marks)

levels.descriptor: Gives incorrect or irrelevant reasoning (e.g. misapplies Gauss's law, claims field inside conductor is nonzero, or fails to connect charge motion to equilibrium), or does not address the effect of a point charge in the cavity.
levels.label: Insufficient (0 marks)

items.stem: Explain why the electric field inside a hollow conducting sphere is zero when the conductor is in electrostatic equilibrium, and why any excess charge placed on the conductor resides on its outer surface. In your explanation, apply Gauss's law and describe what happens to the distribution of charges and the electric field if a point charge is placed inside the hollow cavity (not touching the conductor).

items.answer:
(a) After contact and separation each identical conducting sphere has +4.0 μC.

(b) You should not expect the plastic (insulating) sphere to end up with +4.0 μC. Insulators do not allow free movement of charge throughout the whole object, so charge cannot redistribute evenly between the two objects. Only a small, localized amount of charge (if any) may be transferred at the contact point; therefore the plastic sphere will not generally carry +4.0 μC and the exact value depends on microscopic transfer at the contact (not equal sharing).

rubric.criteria: Correct calculation of equal charge sharing for conductors and correct explanation of why insulators do not equally share charge

levels.descriptor: Part (a): Shows conservation of charge and divides 8.0 μC equally to obtain 4.0 μC on each conducting sphere. Part (b): Clearly states that an insulator will not allow free charge redistribution so it will not end up with +4.0 μC; explains that only localized transfer may occur and equal sharing does not apply.
levels.label: Full marks

levels.descriptor: Part (a): Correct numerical result (4.0 μC) shown but working is minimal or missing units; Part (b): Offers a vague or partially correct explanation (e.g. says insulator 'may not' share charge but gives no reason about lack of free charge movement).
levels.label: Partial credit

levels.descriptor: Part (a): Incorrect calculation (not 4.0 μC) or violates conservation of charge. Part (b): Incorrect statement that the insulator will share charge equally or gives no relevant explanation about charge mobility.
levels.label: No credit

items.stem:
A small metal sphere A is given a total charge of +8.0 μC. It is then touched to an identical, uncharged metal sphere B and the two spheres are separated.

(a) Calculate the final charge on each metal sphere after they are separated. (2 marks)

(b) If sphere B had instead been an identical neutral plastic (insulating) sphere and you repeated the same process (touching the charged metal sphere A to the neutral plastic sphere and then separating them), what charge would you expect on the plastic sphere after separation? Give a numerical answer if possible and explain your reasoning about charge movement in the insulator. (2 marks)
items.working:
(a) Conservation of charge: total initial charge = +8.0 μC + 0 μC = +8.0 μC. Two identical conducting spheres in contact share charge equally because charges are free to move and the spheres have identical capacitance. Final charge on each = total charge / 2 = (8.0 μC) / 2 = 4.0 μC. Units: μC (microcoulombs).

(b) For an insulator, charges are not free to move throughout the object. When the charged metal sphere touches the plastic sphere, there may be only a small, localized transfer of charge at the contact region; charge will not redistribute over the whole plastic sphere. Therefore you cannot calculate a simple equal-sharing value like 4.0 μC; the plastic sphere will not generally end up with +4.0 μC. The exact transferred amount depends on surface properties and is not determined by simple equal sharing.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Mistake: result is ten times too small. A student choosing this likely divided by an extra factor of 10 (decimal-place error) or incorrectly handled powers of ten when multiplying the charges.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Mistake: result is ten times too large. This distractor reflects treating r as 0.50 but forgetting to square it (or misplacing a decimal), giving F ~2.16 N instead of 0.216 N.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Mistake: result is 100 times too small. This choice indicates the student may have squared the charges or introduced an extra factor of 10^-2 when converting microcoulombs, producing an incorrect power-of-ten handling.

items.stem: Two point charges, +3.0 μC and −2.0 μC, are 0.50 m apart in vacuum. Using Coulomb's law (k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2), what is the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them?

items.answer: The electric field is a vector field defined at each point in space that is produced solely by the source charges (the charge distribution). It describes the electrical environment created by those source charges independent of any measurement device. The field E at a point determines the force a test charge will feel, via F = q_test E, so the field is the property of the sources while the force depends on the value of the test charge. Therefore the value of E is independent of which test charge you place there; changing the test charge changes the force but not E. Example: a single point charge Q at the origin produces an electric field E(r) = (1/(4πε0))·(Q / r^2) r̂ (units N C^{-1} or V m^{-1}). If you place a test charge q1 or q2 at distance r, the forces are F1 = q1 E and F2 = q2 E, showing E is the same for both test charges while the forces scale with q.

rubric.criteria: Explanation that the electric field is produced by source charges and is independent of the test charge, supported by F = qE and an illustrative example with units or formula.

levels.descriptor: Complete explanation: defines the electric field as a vector field produced by the source charge distribution, explicitly states that E is independent of the test charge and justifies this using F = q_test E, and gives a correct illustrative example (e.g. point charge formula) including appropriate units or notation.
levels.label: 3 marks

levels.descriptor: Mostly correct: gives a clear definition that E is produced by source charges and states independence from the test charge, and either cites F = qE or gives a correct example (but not both fully developed).
levels.label: 2 marks

levels.descriptor: Partial understanding: makes a relevant statement such as 'E characterises the source charges' or 'the force depends on the test charge' but does not clearly connect these ideas or give a correct example or formula.
levels.label: 1 mark

In your answer, state why the electric field at a point does not depend on the test charge used to measure it, and give one brief physical example (with formula or units) to illustrate.

items.answer: Net electric field = 3.60 × 10^6 N/C directed to the +x (right).

rubric.criteria: Application of the superposition principle and correct vector addition to compute the net electric field (magnitude and direction, with units).

levels.descriptor: Correctly computes both individual field magnitudes with units, determines both field directions correctly, adds them using superposition to give Enet ≈ 3.60 × 10^6 N/C to the +x (right); all arithmetic shown and units carried through.
levels.label: Full marks

levels.descriptor: Correct setup and computation of the two individual field magnitudes (with units) and their directions, but contains an arithmetic or rounding error in the final sum OR gives the correct numeric result but omits units or direction; shows most working.
levels.label: Partial credit

levels.label: Minimal / no credit

items.stem: Two point charges lie on the x-axis: a charge +3.0 μC is at x = 0.00 m and a charge −1.0 μC is at x = +0.20 m. Calculate the net electric field (magnitude and direction) at the point x = +0.10 m. Take k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2. (4 marks)
items.working:
Step 1: Position and distances. The field point is at x = 0.10 m. Distance from +3.0 μC at x=0.00 m is r1 = 0.10 m. Distance from −1.0 μC at x=0.20 m is r2 = 0.10 m.

Step 2: Electric field magnitude from each charge using E = k|q|/r^2.
For q1 = +3.0 μC = +3.0 × 10^−6 C:
E1 = k|q1|/r1^2 = (8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2)(3.0 × 10^−6 C)/(0.10 m)^2
    = (8.99 × 10^9)(3.0 × 10^−6)/(0.01) N/C
    = (8.99 × 10^9)(3.0 × 10^−4) N/C
    = 2.697 × 10^6 N/C.
Direction: q1 is positive, so field at a point to its right is away from q1 → to the +x direction.

For q2 = −1.0 μC = −1.0 × 10^−6 C:
E2 = k|q2|/r2^2 = (8.99 × 10^9)(1.0 × 10^−6)/(0.10^2)
    = (8.99 × 10^9)(1.0 × 10^−4) N/C
    = 8.99 × 10^5 N/C.
Direction: q2 is negative, so the field points toward q2. The field point is to the left of q2, so the field at the point is to the +x direction.

Step 3: Superpose (vector sum). Both fields point in +x direction, so magnitudes add:
Enet = E1 + E2 = 2.697 × 10^6 N/C + 8.99 × 10^5 N/C = 3.596 × 10^6 N/C.

Step 4: Report with suitable sig figs.
Enet ≈ 3.60 × 10^6 N/C to the +x (right).

items.answer: Field lines are drawn so their tangent at any point shows the field direction; the number of lines per area indicates field strength; lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges. Reason: At each point the tangent to a field line equals the electric field direction; line density (lines per unit area perpendicular to them) measures |E|, and by convention lines originate on positive charges and terminate on negative charges.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Correct — this states the three standard rules: (1) tangent gives local direction of E, (2) density of lines per unit area perpendicular to lines represents field magnitude, and (3) lines originate on positive and terminate on negative charges.
options.text: Field lines are drawn so their tangent at any point shows the field direction; the number of lines per area indicates field strength; lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is incorrect because field lines do not cross (crossing would imply two different directions of E at one point); arrows do show the direction a positive test charge would feel a force but the spacing is not arbitrary — it represents field strength.
options.text: Field lines always cross where the field is strongest; arrows on lines show the direction a positive test charge will move and the spacing of lines is arbitrary.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is incorrect because field lines are not necessarily circular around every charge (they are radial for isolated point charges); density represents field strength, not particle speed, and lines start on positive charges, not negative.
options.text: Field lines are circular around every charge; their density indicates the speed a charged particle will have and they always begin on negative charges.

options.rationale: This is incorrect because field lines are perpendicular to equipotentials at every point (not only at infinity) and they do indicate both direction and relative strength, not merely connectivity.

items.stem: A uniform electric field of magnitude E = 5.0 × 10^3 N/C is directed at an angle of 30.0° to the normal of a small flat square surface element of area ΔS = 2.0 cm^2. items.working:
Step 1: Convert area to metres squared.
ΔS = 2.0 cm^2 × (1 × 10^-2 m / 1 cm)^2 = 2.0 × 10^-4 m^2.
Step 2: Write formula for flux through a surface element with angle θ between field and area normal:
Φ = E ΔS cos θ.
Step 3: Substitute numbers (carry units):
E = 5.0 × 10^3 N/C, ΔS = 2.0 × 10^-4 m^2, θ = 30.0°.
Φ = (5.0 × 10^3 N/C) × (2.0 × 10^-4 m^2) × cos(30.0°).
Compute product before cosine: (5.0 × 10^3)(2.0 × 10^-4) = 1.00 (units N·m^2/C).
cos 30.0° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866025.
Φ = 1.00 × 0.866025 N·m^2/C ≈ 0.866 N·m^2/C.

items.stem: Two point charges are in the xy-plane: q1 = +2.0 μC at r1 = (0.00 i + 0.03 j + 0.00 k) m and q2 = −3.0 μC at r2 = (0.04 i + 0.00 j + 0.00 k) m. Using Coulomb's law in vector form, calculate the electrostatic force on q1 due to q2. Give the force as a vector with units and state briefly whether the force is attractive or repulsive. (k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2)
items.working:
1. Write Coulomb's law (vector form) for force on q1 due to q2: F = k q1 q2 (r1 − r2)/|r1 − r2|^3.
2. Compute charge product and convert μC to C: q1 = 2.0 μC = 2.0×10^−6 C, q2 = −3.0 μC = −3.0×10^−6 C; q1 q2 = (2.0×10^−6)(−3.0×10^−6) = −6.0×10^−12 C^2.
3. Compute displacement vector r1 − r2: r1 − r2 = (0.00 − 0.04, 0.03 − 0.00, 0.00 − 0.00) m = (−0.04, 0.03, 0.00) m.
4. Compute separation magnitude: |r1 − r2| = sqrt((−0.04)^2 + (0.03)^2) m = sqrt(0.0016 + 0.0009) m = sqrt(0.0025) m = 0.05 m.
5. Compute |r1 − r2|^3 = (0.05 m)^3 = 0.000125 m^3.
6. Compute scalar prefactor: k q1 q2 / |r|^3 = (8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2)(−6.0×10^−12 C^2) / 0.000125 m^3
   = (−5.394×10^−2 N·m^2) / 0.000125 m^3 = −431.52 N/m.
   (Units reduce to N/m times m gives N when multiplied by r-vector components.)
7. Multiply by r-vector to get force: F = (−431.52 N/m) × (−0.04, 0.03, 0.00) m = (17.2608, −12.9456, 0.0000) N.
8. Round to three significant figures: F ≈ (17.26 i − 12.95 j + 0.00 k) N.
9. Sign/physical interpretation: q2 has opposite sign to q1, so the force on q1 is attractive; the vector points from q1 toward q2 (which matches the computed components).

items.stem: Three point charges lie on the x-axis: q1 = +5.0 μC at x = 0.00 m, q2 = -3.0 μC at x = 0.20 m, and q3 = +2.0 μC at x = −0.15 m. Using Coulomb's law and the principle of superposition, calculate the net electrostatic force on q2. Give the answer as a vector along the x-axis (include magnitude, direction, and units). Use k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2.
items.working:
Step 1: Convert charges to coulombs.
q1 = +5.0 μC = +5.0 × 10^-6 C
q2 = −3.0 μC = −3.0 × 10^-6 C
q3 = +2.0 μC = +2.0 × 10^-6 C

Step 2: Find distances along x between q2 and the other charges (use magnitudes).
Distance r12 between q1 (x=0.00 m) and q2 (x=0.20 m): r12 = 0.20 m
Distance r32 between q3 (x=−0.15 m) and q2 (x=0.20 m): r32 = 0.20 − (−0.15) = 0.35 m

Step 3: Compute magnitude of force on q2 due to q1 using Coulomb's law (scalar magnitude).
F_12 = k |q1 q2| / r12^2 = (8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2) × (|5.0 × 10^-6 C × 3.0 × 10^-6 C|) / (0.20 m)^2
= 8.99 × 10^9 × (15.0 × 10^-12 C^2) / 0.04 m^2
= 8.99 × 10^9 × 3.75 × 10^-10 N
= 3.37125 N
Direction: q1 is positive and q2 is negative ⇒ attraction toward q1 (which is at smaller x), so force on q2 is toward negative x. Represent as F_12 = −3.37125 i N.

Step 4: Compute magnitude of force on q2 due to q3.
F_32 = k |q3 q2| / r32^2 = (8.99 × 10^9) × (|2.0 × 10^-6 × 3.0 × 10^-6|) / (0.35)^2
= 8.99 × 10^9 × (6.0 × 10^-12) / 0.1225
= 8.99 × 10^9 × 4.8980 × 10^-11 N
= 0.4405 N (approximately)
Direction: q3 is positive and q2 is negative ⇒ attraction toward q3 (which is at smaller x), so force on q2 is toward negative x. Represent as F_32 = −0.4405 i N.

Step 5: Superpose (vector sum) the two forces (both along x, both negative):
F_net = F_12 + F_32 = (−3.37125 − 0.4405) i N = −3.81175 i N.

Step 6: Report with appropriate significant figures (given data to three significant figures):
F_net ≈ −3.81 i N, i.e. 3.81 N toward the negative x-direction.

items.answer: (a) Charge transferred = (5.0 × 10^12 electrons) × (1.60 × 10^-19 C per electron) = 8.0 × 10^-7 C. Object A loses these electrons so it gains positive charge +8.0 × 10^-7 C. Object B gains these electrons so it gains negative charge −8.0 × 10^-7 C. (b) The net charge = (+8.0 × 10^-7 C) + (−8.0 × 10^-7 C) = 0 C. At the atomic scale rubbing transfers discrete electrons from atoms on A to atoms on B; no charges are created or destroyed, only redistributed. Because free charge occurs in integer multiples of the electron charge (q = n e) the transferred charge is exactly n·e with n = 5.0 × 10^12, so each object’s charge is a whole-number multiple of e. Therefore rubbing moves existing electrons between the objects but does not change the total charge of the isolated system.

items.stem: Two neutral insulating objects A and B are rubbed together and, as a result, 5.0 × 10^12 electrons are transferred from object A to object B. (a) Calculate the electric charge on object A and on object B after the rubbing. (b) Calculate the net charge of the two-object system and explain, using atomic-scale charge transfer and the quantisation of charge, why rubbing transfers electrons but does not create net charge. (Use the electron charge magnitude e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C.)
items.working: Step 1: Number of electrons transferred n = 5.0 × 10^12 (given). Step 2: Electron charge e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C (given). Step 3: Magnitude of transferred charge q = n · e = (5.0 × 10^12) × (1.60 × 10^-19 C) = 8.0 × 10^-7 C. Step 4: Object A loses electrons → charge on A = +q = +8.0 × 10^-7 C. Step 5: Object B gains electrons → charge on B = −q = −8.0 × 10^-7 C. Step 6: Net charge = (+8.0 × 10^-7 C) + (−8.0 × 10^-7 C) = 0 C. Step 7: Explanation: rubbing removes electrons from atomic orbitals on A and deposits them on B; these are discrete electrons so the transferred charge is an integer multiple of e (quantisation). No charges are created or destroyed in the process, only redistributed, so the net charge remains zero (conservation of charge).

items.answer: On axis: E = (1/4πϵ0) (2p / r^3) ẑ; Equatorial plane: E = - (1/4πϵ0) (p / r^3) ẑ. Reason: p = 2aq, expand the exact two-charge field to leading order for r >> a; monopole terms cancel and the dipole term gives a field ~1/r^3 with coefficients 2p on-axis and −p in the equatorial plane (SI units, with 1/(4πϵ0)).

options.label: A
options.rationale: Correct. For r >> a, expand the fields to leading order: on the axis the dipole field is E = (1/4πϵ0)(2p/r^3) along +z (away from center toward +q), and in the equatorial plane the field is E = -(1/4πϵ0)(p/r^3) ẑ (toward the dipole axis, opposite the dipole moment). Both have the 1/r^3 dependence and use p = 2aq.
options.text: On axis: E = (1/4πϵ0) (2p / r^3) ẑ (pointing away from the center toward +q). Equatorial plane: E = - (1/4πϵ0) (p / r^3) ẑ (pointing opposite to the dipole moment).

options.label: B
options.rationale: Incorrect: This option shows a 1/r^2 dependence. The far-field dipole field falls off as 1/r^3, so using 1/r^2 is the wrong radial scaling (confuses dipole with monopole field).
options.text: On axis: E = (1/4πϵ0) (p / r^2) ẑ. Equatorial plane: E = - (1/4πϵ0) (p / r^2) ẑ.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Incorrect: Although the axial expression gives the correct 1/r^3 scaling, the equatorial field sign/direction is wrong (it should be opposite the dipole moment, i.e., −ẑ). Also using r̂ for axial points is confusing here; the axial result should be written along ẑ with the correct sign.
options.text: On axis: E = (1/4πϵ0) (2p / r^3) r̂ where r̂ points radially outward from the center; Equatorial plane: E = (1/4πϵ0) (p / r^3) r̂ pointing outward in the plane.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Incorrect: Both signs are flipped. On the axis toward +q the field points away from the center (positive ẑ) so the axial field should be +2p/(4πϵ0 r^3) ẑ, not negative; the equatorial field should be opposite to p (−p/(4πϵ0 r^3) ẑ), not along +ẑ.

items.answer:
Linear charge density λ: λ = dQ/dl, where dQ is the charge contained in an infinitesimal length element dl along a charged line. SI unit: coulomb per metre (C·m⁻¹).

Surface charge density σ: σ = dQ/dA, where dQ is the charge contained in an infinitesimal area element dA on a charged surface. SI unit: coulomb per square metre (C·m⁻²).

Volume charge density ρ: ρ = dQ/dV, where dQ is the charge contained in an infinitesimal volume element dV in a charged volume. SI unit: coulomb per cubic metre (C·m⁻³).

- Use E(r) = k Q / r^2.
- Compute r^2 = (0.20 m)^2 = 0.0400 m^2.
- Compute numerator: k Q = (8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2)(5.0 × 10^−6 C) = 8.99 × 5.0 × 10^3 N·m^2/C = 44.95 × 10^3 N·m^2/C = 4.495 × 10^4 N·m^2/C.
- Divide: E = (4.495 × 10^4 N·m^2/C) / (0.0400 m^2) = 1.12375 × 10^6 N/C ≈ 1.12 × 10^6 N/C.
- Direction: Q is positive, so E is radially outward from the origin.

items.answer: Magnitude of electric field at the midpoint: 1.80 × 10^6 N/C, directed from the positive charge toward the negative charge (i.e. toward the −1.0 μC charge).

rubric.criteria: Correct magnitude (with units) and correct direction of the electric field at the midpoint, using Coulomb's law and distances.

levels.descriptor: Correct numerical magnitude (3.60 × 10^6 N/C) with units and correct direction (toward the −1.0 μC charge). Working shows E = k|q|/r^2 for each charge with r = 0.100 m, correct arithmetic for both fields, and correct vector addition.
levels.label: Full credit

levels.descriptor: Correct method (uses E = k|q|/r^2 with r = 0.100 m and identifies directions of individual fields) but one arithmetic sign or numerical error that leads to a magnitude differing by about a factor of 2 (e.g. gives 1.80 × 10^6 N/C) or missing units; direction may be correct or unclear. Working shows most steps.
levels.label: Partial credit

levels.descriptor: Incorrect method (no use of Coulomb's law at midpoint, wrong distance used), or answer is a number with no units and no supporting working, or direction is opposite and incompatible with shown calculations.
levels.label: Minimal/no credit

items.stem: Two point charges, +3.0 μC and −1.0 μC, are fixed 20.0 cm apart on a horizontal line. Find the magnitude and direction of the electric field at the point midway between them. State the result with appropriate units and show your working.
items.working:
Let the charges be q1 = +3.0 μC = +3.0 × 10^-6 C (left) and q2 = −1.0 μC = −1.0 × 10^-6 C (right). Separation d = 20.0 cm = 0.200 m, so midpoint is r = d/2 = 0.100 m from each charge.
Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2.
Magnitude of field from q1 at midpoint: E1 = k |q1| / r^2 = (8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2)(3.0 × 10^-6 C) / (0.100 m)^2
= (8.99 × 10^9)(3.0 × 10^-6) / 0.0100
= (8.99 × 10^9 × 3.0 × 10^-6) × 100
= (8.99 × 3.0 × 10^3) N/C
= 2.697 × 10^6 N/C.
Direction: q1 is positive so its field at the midpoint points away from q1, i.e. to the right (toward q2).
Magnitude of field from q2 at midpoint: E2 = k |q2| / r^2 = (8.99 × 10^9)(1.0 × 10^-6) / (0.100)^2
= (8.99 × 10^9 × 1.0 × 10^-6) / 0.0100
= (8.99 × 10^9 × 1.0 × 10^-6) × 100
= 8.99 × 10^5 N/C.
Direction: q2 is negative so its field at the midpoint points toward q2, i.e. to the right as well.
Since both fields at the midpoint point to the right, net field magnitude is E = E1 + E2? (Careful: fields due to positive and negative charges point in same direction here.) Numerically: E_net = 2.697 × 10^6 N/C + 8.99 × 10^5 N/C = 3.596 × 10^6 N/C.
However, check signs consistently: if we take right as positive, E1 (from +3 μC) = +2.697 × 10^6 N/C, E2 (from −1 μC) = +8.99 × 10^5 N/C, so E_net = +3.596 × 10^6 N/C to the right.
But note: the fields above used r = 0.100 m; if instead one considers directions with respect to each source correctly, the field from the negative charge points toward it (right) with magnitude 8.99 × 10^5 N/C, and the field from the positive charge points away from it (right) with magnitude 2.697 × 10^6 N/C. Therefore E_net = 2.697 × 10^6 − 8.99 × 10^5 = 1.798 × 10^6 N/C to the right if one had mistakenly taken one as opposite. The correct physical reasoning shows both point to the right, so the correct sum is 3.596 × 10^6 N/C to the right.
Final answer (corrected with consistent sign and direction): E_net = 3.60 × 10^6 N/C, directed toward the −1.0 μC charge (to the right).

classification.chapter: Electrostatics / Electric Field and Gauss's Law
classification.subject: Physics
classification.topic: Electrostatics (charges, Coulomb's law, electric field, flux, Gauss's law)

bullet_points: insulator: A material that offers high resistance to the passage of electricity and in which charge placed remains localized rather than spreading.
At atomic scale: electrons move between materials; protons remain in nuclei.
Rubbing transfers electrons from one object to another — it does NOT create net charge.
Conductors: charges are comparatively free to move; insulators: charges stay localized.
Conservation of charge: in an isolated system the total electric charge is conserved; charge may be redistributed but the net charge remains constant.
Next: quantisation of charge → then Coulomb's law (magnitude & vector)
diagrams_to_draw: Simple atom: small circle labelled 'nucleus (protons + neutrons)' and one or two electrons drawn and labelled 'electron (negative)'.
Electroscope sketch: knob and two leaves, with leaves apart after contact; arrow pointing from rubbed rod to knob showing electron transfer.
Comb near paperclip: comb with '-' signs on its surface and induced '+' signs on the nearer end of the paperclip (no formula, just signs to show transfer/induction).

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Electrons move from one material to the other. Specifically, if glass loses electrons to silk, the glass has fewer electrons than protons and becomes net positive while the silk gains electrons and becomes net negative. (State which material in your classroom example gained electrons.)
checkpoint_questions.question: You rub a glass rod with silk. At the atomic scale, which particles move and in which direction (qualitatively)?

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: The plastic rod (an insulator) is more likely to keep its charge because charges remain localized; the metal sphere (a conductor) lets charges move and leak to ground through contact so it loses charge. Mention that in the conductor electrons travel to ground but in the insulator they stay stuck where transferred.
checkpoint_questions.question: A metal sphere and a plastic rod are both rubbed and then touched to the floor. Which one is more likely to keep its charge and why, in terms of charge mobility?

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: The net charge before and after rubbing is the same. If after rubbing the charges are +2 μC and −2 μC, their sum is 0 μC, so no net charge was created; charge was redistributed (electrons moved) between the objects.
checkpoint_questions.question: If you rub two objects together and one becomes +2 μC and the other −2 μC, what does this tell you about the net charge before and after rubbing? Use conservation of charge in your answer.

entry_ticket.expected_response: Most correct response: B — rubbing transfers electrons so the balloon gains negative charge and something else loses the same amount; no net charge is created. A common wrong response: A or C, written with reasons like 'rubbing makes charge' or 'hair makes charge'.
entry_ticket.prompt:
You rub a dry balloon on your hair. After rubbing, the balloon sticks to the wall. Circle which statement you think is true, and briefly say why (one sentence):
A) Rubbing the balloon created new electric charge on the balloon and on the wall.
B) Rubbing moved existing charge so the balloon gained negative charge and some other object lost the same amount of negative charge.
C) The balloon became charged only because your hair produced charge from nowhere.
(Write A, B, or C and one short reason.)

exit_ticket.prompt: In one short paragraph, explain using atomic-scale evidence why rubbing two materials transfers electrons and does not create net charge. Include which particle moves, how the two objects' signs change, and one concrete classroom example (e.g., comb and paper).
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Mentions that electrons (not protons) move from one material to the other; states that one object becomes net negative and the other net positive; explicitly says the algebraic sum of charges is unchanged (gives an example like +q and −q or states net charge remains same); gives a concrete example (comb and paper or glass and silk).

homework.submission_format: Handwritten or typed page with one labelled diagram and the short observation paragraph; bring to the next class.
tasks: Write a one-page explanation (≈300 words) using an atomic picture to describe what happens when a nylon comb is rubbed on dry hair. Draw and label a simple diagram showing electrons moving and indicate the final net charge on each object with units.

Measure and record one real example at home: rub a clean plastic comb on dry hair, bring it near small bits of paper, and note whether paper is attracted. In one paragraph, connect your observation to the atomic-scale electron transfer you drew above.

Short quiz question (answer on the same sheet): Two identical insulating balloons are rubbed on wool. Afterward they repel each other. Propose two possible distributions of charge on the balloons (numbers with units) that are consistent with conservation of charge and explain why both are possible.

mentor_moment.story: A physics teacher once combed a volunteer's hair in front of the class; the comb picked up bits of paper and stuck to a metal tray until the tray was grounded and the effect vanished.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Seeing a comb attract paper shows charge moved to the comb; touching the metal tray to ground removed the charge—conservation means charge moved away, not disappeared.
mentor_moment.title: The Workshop Comb Surprise

anticipated_questions: What if a balloon is neutral after rubbing? (Students may ask if rubbing always charges.)
How can we tell which object lost electrons? (Students want to know direction of transfer.)
Does the wall get charged if it is plaster or painted? (Asking about material differences.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write: "Entry ticket: A / B / C" and tally two example answers under each as you read them aloud.
teacher_script.heading: Collect responses and surface the key belief
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Turn your paper over so I can see your letter and one-line reason. Hold it up when I call your row." Walk to the first row, pick two student answers to read aloud (one that picked B and one that picked A/C). Then say: "Thanks — we will check which view fits the evidence. Keep your paper — we may return to it."

anticipated_questions: How many electrons move? (Students wonder about magnitude — answer: varies; we will not calculate charge yet.)
Why don't protons move? (Answer: protons are bound in nuclei and much more tightly held.)
What makes electrons move from one material to another? (Lead into next beat: different materials hold electrons with different strengths.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw a simple atom: small labeled nucleus and orbiting electrons; label 'electron (negative)' and 'proton in nucleus (positive)'. Underline: 'electrons can move between materials; protons do not'.
teacher_script.heading: Introduce electric charge at the atomic scale
teacher_script.speaker_notes:
Say: "At the atomic level, some particles — electrons — carry negative charge and can move between materials. Protons stay fixed in atomic nuclei. When two materials touch and rub, electrons can move from atoms in one material to atoms in the other. That is a transfer of existing electrons — not creation of new charge." Point to the diagram of an atom and label electron and nucleus. Then ask: "Which particle moves during rubbing, electron or proton?" Wait for the answer and confirm: "Electron."
Then say: "So when a balloon picks up extra electrons, it becomes negatively charged by gain of electrons; the object that lost those electrons becomes positively charged by the same amount."

anticipated_questions: Where did the electrons come from? (Answer: from the fur or the rod depending on which material loses electrons.)
If I ground the electroscope, what happens? (Answer: ground provides a path for electrons to leave or enter; next step shows leaves collapse.)
Does the electroscope show positive vs negative? (Answer: it shows net charge magnitude via leaf separation; sign depends on which object was touched.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the sequence of actions as short bullets: 'uncharged electroscope → rub rod → touch electroscope → leaves separate'. Draw a simple electroscope sketch with leaves apart after charging.
teacher_script.heading: Teacher demonstration: rubbing and showing transfer
teacher_script.speaker_notes:
Perform demonstration: Use a nylon rod and fur, and an electroscope (or a small aluminium foil leaf electroscope). Steps aloud as you do them:
1) "Show the uncharged electroscope: leaves hang close together." Place the rod nearby without touching — note no effect.
2) "Now rub the nylon rod with the fur for 20 seconds." Rub the rod visibly while students watch.
3) "Touch the electroscope knob briefly with the rubbed rod." Touch and then step back and point: "The leaves separate — that shows charge was transferred to the electroscope."
4) "Tap the electroscope to ground it and then touch again with the rod to show charging by contact repeats." Ask: "Did we create net charge inside the room?" Wait for answers and guide to: "No — we moved electrons from one object to another; the total charge in the closed system stayed the same."

anticipated_questions: Why did the paperclip stick sometimes but not always? (Answer: induced charge or grounding; also humidity and contact matter.)
Can the metal become charged? (Answer: yes, but it conducts so charge spreads or leaks to ground.)
If the comb is an insulator why does it attract the metal? (Answer: comb holds charge locally; it induces opposite charge in metal causing attraction.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write instructions briefly: 'Combine: comb + hair → bring near paperclip (no touch) → touch paperclip'. Underneath write: 'Observe: attraction? leaves? charge retention?'.
teacher_script.heading: Mini-lab: short guided pairing to test conductors vs insulators
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "In pairs, take a plastic comb and a small metal paperclip. Rub the comb on your hair for 15 seconds, then bring it near the paperclip (not touching). Observe what happens. Then touch the comb briefly to one end of the paperclip and observe. 3 minutes to do this; I will circulate." After 3 minutes call them back and ask two pairs to report: what happened near the paperclip, and what happened after touching. Key point to elicit: comb (an insulator) can hold localized charge and attract the paperclip; metal paperclip conducts and any charge given to it flows and may be shared or lost to teacher's grounded table.

anticipated_questions: What does 'net' charge mean? (Answer: sum of positive and negative — if electrons are moved within the system total doesn't change.)
Can rubbing create equal numbers of positive and negative charges? (Guide to: charges are transferred as electrons; you do not create new positive or negative out of nothing.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the three key words students must include: 'electrons', 'transfer', 'conserved (net unchanged)'.
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice: explain rubbing as transfer, not creation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Project or write this prompt and call on volunteers: "Explain in 30 seconds why rubbing does not create net charge. Use the terms electrons, transfer, and conservation." Call on 3 students. For each response, give a one-sentence corrective comment: e.g. 'Good — you named electrons and transfer; add that the other object loses the same number of electrons so net charge is unchanged.'

anticipated_questions: Will we calculate forces next time? (Answer: yes — Coulomb's law gives magnitude and vector later.)
Do we ever get neutral objects after contact? (Answer: yes, if net transfer cancels; we will discuss how to measure net charge later.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write two short bullets linking forward: 'Next: quantisation of charge' and 'Then: Coulomb's law'.
teacher_script.heading: Check for understanding and link forward
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Quick quiz: True or false — An insulator cannot become charged. Hold up T or F." Scan responses; then say: "Correct answer: False. Insulators can acquire and hold charge locally. Conductors let charges move and may leak to ground. Next period we will use these ideas to explain why charge comes in packets (quantisation) and to derive the mathematical form of Coulomb's law." Collect one final verbal summary from the class: 'Charge is electrons moving; rubbing transfers electrons; total charge conserved.'

bullet_points: Learning goal: Use quantisation and conservation to derive Coulomb's law and explain rubbing as transfer of electrons.
point charge: A charge whose linear size is very small compared to distances considered; all the charge is treated as concentrated at a single point.
Quantisation of charge: q = n e    (q in coulombs, n integer, e = elementary charge)
Scalar Coulomb's law: F = (1/4πε0) q1 q2 / r^2    (F in N, q in C, r in m)
Vector Coulomb's law: F_12 = (1/4πε0) (q1 q2 / r_12^2) r_hat_21    (direction along line joining charges)
Sphere example: identical uncharged spheres touching charged spheres -> charges split equally by symmetry (q -> q/2).
Algebra from example: F' = (1/4πε0)(q/2)(q'/2)/(r/2)^2 = (1/4πε0) q q' / r^2 = F
Guided practice setups written (no long arithmetic).
Summary: q = n e; Coulomb magnitude depends on product of charges and inverse square of separation; vector form gives direction and sign (attract/repel).
diagrams_to_draw: Four spheres: A(q) touching C(0) -> separate -> A(q/2), C(q/2). Similarly B(q') and D(0) -> B(q'/2), D(q'/2). Show centre-to-centre separation labelled r and r/2.
