Two point charges at r1 (q1) and r2 (q2) with arrow r_hat_21 pointing from charge 2 toward charge 1 to indicate direction of force on 1.
Quick coordinate sketch for guided practice problems showing two charges and separation with labels.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Electrons moved from the glass to the silk (or from the silk to the glass depending on materials), leaving the glass deficient by 3e; charge was transferred between bodies so no new net charge was created — total charge is conserved.
checkpoint_questions.question: You rub a glass rod with silk and the rod ends up with net +3e (three elementary charges). Explain, in one sentence, what happened to electrons and why no new charge was created.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Stays the same: product q1 q2 is unchanged because +2e × -4e = +2e × (-2e + -2e) summed equals the same total product; Coulomb magnitude depends on the total product and separation, so force magnitude is unchanged.
checkpoint_questions.question: Two point charges q1 = +2e and q2 = -4e are 0.50 m apart in vacuum. Without calculating numbers, state whether the force magnitude on q1 due to q2 increases, decreases, or stays the same if q2 is replaced by two separate point charges each -2e placed at the same location. Explain briefly.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: F_12 = (1/4πϵ0) (q1 q2 / r_{12}^2) r̂_{21}; the unit vector r̂_{21} points from q1 toward q2 (i.e., along the line joining them, direction of the force on q1 due to q2).
checkpoint_questions.question: Write the vector expression for the force on charge q1 at position r1 due to charge q2 at r2, and identify the unit vector direction in words.

entry_ticket.expected_response: C — electrons are transferred from one object to the other; no new net charge is created. (Reason: rubbing moves electrons between materials; total charge before and after is the same.)
entry_ticket.prompt: You rub a plastic comb on dry hair. Do you think the comb has: (A) gained new charge that did not exist before, (B) lost some charge that disappears, or (C) had electrons transferred from the hair so total charge is conserved? Pick A, B or C and one sentence why.

exit_ticket.prompt: A student says: 'Rubbing a plastic comb on hair creates new charge out of nowhere because the comb becomes charged.' In two sentences, correct the student's statement using atomic-scale charge transfer and state the relevant formula for charge quantisation.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Student states that rubbing transfers electrons between materials (identifying which object loses/gains electrons) so total net charge is conserved, and writes q = n e with n an integer; answer correctly links transfer to conservation rather than creation.

homework.submission_format: handwritten solutions scanned or photographed and uploaded
tasks: 1) Two identical small conducting spheres, A and B, are isolated. A has net charge +6e and B is neutral. The spheres are touched together and then separated. (a) What is the charge on each afterward? Show arithmetic with units. (b) If the separation between A and a fixed third charge C is then halved, explain quantitatively how the Coulomb force between A and C changes (use the scalar Coulomb formula).

2) Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between q1 = -3e and q2 = +5e separated by 0.20 m in vacuum. Show all steps, carry units (C, m, N), and use e = 1.602×10^-19 C and 1/4πε0 = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2.

3) Draw two point charges of equal magnitude and opposite sign separated by 0.30 m. On the diagram, draw and label the force vector acting on the positive charge due to the negative one (include direction and write the vector form using r̂).

mentor_moment.story: I once rubbed a balloon on a sweater until it stuck to a wall; the balloon lost a tiny number of electrons to the sweater, not 'made' charge. The wall and balloon then attract because of redistributed charges and Coulomb forces.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Friction moves electrons between materials; conservation means rubbing transfers charge, and Coulomb's law predicts the resulting force direction and size.
mentor_moment.title: The sweater-and-balloon trick

anticipated_questions: Why must we decide between those three options now?
What do you mean by 'atomic-scale reasoning'?
If electrons move, doesn't that create charge somewhere else?
teacher_script.board_action: Write at top: "Learning goal: Use quantisation and conservation to derive Coulomb's law and explain rubbing as transfer of electrons."
teacher_script.heading: Collect entry tickets & announce learning goal
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Collect a quick show of hands: how many chose A, B, C? (Pause for hands.) "Good — we will keep that idea in mind. Today we will use the idea that charge is conserved and quantised to find the force between point charges: Coulomb's law. By the end you should be able to explain, with atomic-scale reasoning, why rubbing transfers electrons and does not create net charge."

anticipated_questions: Why do the charges split exactly in half? (Because spheres are identical so capacitances equal; by symmetry and conservation charges equalize.)
Do we need to measure electrons to say q/2? (No — conservation + symmetry gives distribution.)
If they touch briefly, how fast does this happen? (Very quickly compared to our experiment; we treat final distribution only.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw four spheres labelled A(q), C(0) touching then separate -> A(q/2), C(q/2). Similarly B(q'), D(0) -> B(q'/2), D(q'/2). Draw arrow showing original separation r then r/2. Write short note: "Charge conserved in contact; identical spheres => equal split."
teacher_script.heading: Measured demonstration: identical spheres A,B,C,D
teacher_script.speaker_notes: I will show a diagram and talk you through a thought experiment you can imagine as spheres in the lab. Say sphere A has charge q and sphere B has charge q'. Two identical uncharged spheres C and D touch A and B respectively, then are separated so each pair shares charge by symmetry. Ask: "If C touches A and they are identical, what charge does each have afterwards?" (Wait for answers: q/2.) "Why? Because charge is conserved and the spheres are identical so charge distributes equally. Same for B and D: q' becomes q'/2 on each.)" Then point to the next question: "If the centre-to-centre distance between the original charged spheres A and B is halved, what happens to the force between the charges on A and B if we first replace A and B by the halves q/2 and q'/2?" Let students estimate before we calculate.

anticipated_questions: Where did 1/4πε0 come from? (It is the experimentally determined constant for vacuum permittivity; we use it as measured. We will not derive its value now.)

Why does the algebra keep the force the same when both charge halves and distance halves? (Because halving charges multiplies numerator by 1/4, while halving r squares to 1/4 in denominator, cancelling.)
Does this always work for non-spherical objects? (Coulomb's inverse-square form applies to point charges; for extended bodies you must treat charge distribution.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write formula stepwise: F = (1/4πε0) q q' / r^2. Then write replacement: F' = (1/4πε0) (q/2)(q'/2) / (r/2)^2. Show algebraic simplification to F' = q q'/(4πε0 r^2). Underline units: q (C), r (m), F (N).
teacher_script.heading: Introduce Coulomb's law (magnitude) by derivation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Write the scalar form we will derive from experiments: F = (1/4πε0) q1 q2 / r^2. Now show the calculation for the sphere example. "Original force between A and B: F = (1/4πε0) q q' / r^2." Then after touching and halving charges and halving separation: compute F' = (1/4πε0) (q/2)(q'/2) / (r/2)^2. Work it out step by step on the board: numerator (q q'/4); denominator (r^2 /4). Simplify: (q q'/4) / (r^2 /4) = q q' / r^2, so F' = F. Say aloud each algebra step and keep units: q in coulombs (C), r in metres (m), force in newtons (N), 1/4πε0 has units N·m^2/C^2. Conclude: this is consistent with an inverse-square law proportional to product of charges. Say: "This is the same algebra we use to motivate the scalar Coulomb law from experiment."

anticipated_questions: Why r_hat_21 and not r_hat_12? (Because the formula uses the unit vector pointing from source to the point where force is evaluated; we will stick to the source notation.)
What if both charges are negative? (Product q1 q2 positive -> repulsion; direction given by unit vector still yields correct orientation.)
Do we need ε0's numeric value? (Only for numerical answers; for understanding symbolic form we do not compute it now.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw two points labelled r1 (q1) and r2 (q2). Draw arrow r_hat_21 pointing from 2 to 1. Write definition of point charge. Write vector formula exactly as given in source.
teacher_script.heading: Derive vector form of Coulomb's law
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Introduce the point charge definition: read aloud: "point charge: A charge whose linear size is very small compared to distances considered; all the charge is treated as concentrated at a single point." Draw two point charges q1 at position r1 and q2 at r2. Ask: "Which direction is the force on q1 due to q2?" (Expect answers toward or away along the line joining them depending on signs.) Explain: "The force acts along the line joining the charges; sign of q1 q2 gives attraction (negative product) or repulsion (positive product)." Write the vector formula: F_12 = (1/4πε0) (q1 q2 / r_12^2) r_hat_21. Define r_12 as the magnitude of r1 - r2 and r_hat_21 as the unit vector pointing from 1 to 2? (Clarify: use the source's notation: r_12 is the distance between charges; r_hat_21 is the unit vector pointing from charge 2 toward charge 1 so direction on force on 1.) Work a quick sign example: q1=+1.0×10^-6 C at left, q2= -2.0×10^-6 C at right separated by 0.50 m; direction is toward q2. Do a short calculation of magnitude with units: compute F magnitude = (1/4πε0)(|q1||q2|)/r^2. Use ε0 = 8.85×10^-12 C^2/(N·m^2) if students ask for numbers, but avoid long arithmetic — show units confirm N.

anticipated_questions: Should we include signs in the magnitude? (No — magnitude is positive; sign/direction comes from vector form.)
How do we show the unit vector numerically? (We write the unit vector symbolically for direction; to get components you need coordinates.)
Can we plug ε0 now? (Yes if you want a numerical answer; not required for the set-up.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write setups: F = (1/4πε0)( (2.0e-6)(3.0e-6) / (0.30)^2 ) N and F = (1/4πε0)( (1.0e-6)(1.0e-6) / (0.20)^2 ) r_hat_21 with note: second is attraction so arrow points toward q2.
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice: quick problems
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Hand out or project two quick prompts. Prompt 1: Two point charges q1 = +2.0×10^-6 C and q2 = +3.0×10^-6 C are 0.30 m apart in vacuum. Ask students to estimate whether the force is attraction or repulsion and to set up the magnitude expression. Prompt 2: Two charges q1 = +1.0×10^-6 C and q2 = -1.0×10^-6 C, 0.20 m apart. Ask students to write the vector form showing direction with unit vector. Walk the room for 3 minutes and listen to setups. Reconvene and write one correct setup for each on the board without doing the full arithmetic (unless a student volunteers).

anticipated_questions: What does quantised mean for large objects? (It means total charge is an integer multiple of e; for macroscopic objects n is very large.)
Do we ever see exceptions to conservation in rubbing? (No; measurable transfers are transfers of electrons, not creation of charge.)
Will we use superposition next? (Yes — next period we add contributions from many point charges.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write 3 quick answers with one-line reasons. Final line: "Summary: q = n e; F = (1/4πε0) q1 q2 / r^2; vector form: F_12 = (1/4πε0) (q1 q2 / r_12^2) r_hat_21."
teacher_script.heading: Formative check and consolidate
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Ask three quick exit questions out loud and have students write A/B/C on a mini whiteboard: 1) "If you rub two materials, is new net charge created? A Yes B No" (Correct: B, with short explanation: electrons transfer.) 2) "Does Coulomb's magnitude depend on q1q2 or q1+q2? A product B sum" (Correct: A product.) 3) "If distance doubles, how does magnitude change? A doubles B halves C becomes 1/4" (Correct: C becomes 1/4). Collect responses and summarise: "Charge is quantised q = n e and conserved in transfers; Coulomb's law gives magnitude and vector direction along the line between point charges."

bullet_points: Test charge: A charge q used to probe the electric field of a source charge; ideally negligibly small so it does not disturb the source charge distribution.
Superposition (forces): Total electrostatic force = vector sum of individual Coulomb forces from each source charge.
Electric field E at a point: force per unit test charge; E = F/q. Units: N/C.
Superposition (field): Net E = vector sum of E from each point charge.
Electric field lines: tangent = field direction; density ∝ strength; start on +, end on -.
Electric flux through area element ΔS: ΔΦ = E·ΔS = E ΔS cosθ. For closed surface, ΔS points outward normal.
Conservation note (rubbing): Electrons move between materials; protons stay in nuclei; rubbing transfers electrons (net charge redistributed), it does not create net charge.
diagrams_to_draw: Two source charges Q1 at x=-d and Q2 at x=+d with test charge q at x=0; draw force vectors F1 and F2 on q.
Single positive point charge with radial field arrows (field lines outward).
Electric dipole sketch (+ and - close together) with field lines and a point in between showing vector addition of fields.
Small flat area element ΔS with normal drawn, angle θ to E vector; label ΔS and θ.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Compute force from each charge using F = (1/4πε0) Q q / r^2, keep directions. r1 = 0.10 m to the right of Q1 so F1 is repulsive → +x. r2 = 0.20 m to the left of Q2 so q is to left of Q2; since Q2 is negative and q positive, force is attractive → +x (toward Q2). Numerical values: k≈8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2. F1 = k(4.0e-6)(1.0e-6)/(0.10^2) ≈ 3.596×10^-1 N to +x. F2 = k(2.0e-6)(1.0e-6)/(0.20^2) ≈ 4.495×10^-2 N to +x. Net F ≈ (0.3596+0.04495) N ≈ 0.4046 N to +x. (Accept answers within few percent.)
checkpoint_questions.question: Two point charges lie on the x-axis: Q1 = +4.0 μC at x = 0.00 m and Q2 = -2.0 μC at x = 0.30 m. A test charge q = +1.0 μC is placed at x = 0.10 m. Using Coulomb-like point-force expression, find the net electrostatic force vector on q (give magnitude in N and direction along +x or -x).

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: No — by definition the electric field is a property of the source-charge distribution and a test charge is ideally negligibly small so it does not disturb that distribution; therefore the field is independent of the test charge used to measure it.
checkpoint_questions.question: A small positive test charge is placed at a point in space near several source charges. The class debates whether moving the test charge changes the field produced by the sources. State whether the field produced by the source charges depends on the test charge and give a one-sentence reason using the definition of test charge.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: At the midpoint the magnitude of the field from each charge is the same since distances are equal. The +Q produces a field pointing away from +Q (toward the negative charge), and the -Q produces a field pointing toward -Q (also toward the negative charge). The magnitudes add (they point in the same direction), so the net field points from the positive toward the negative charge (along the line joining them).
checkpoint_questions.question: At a point exactly halfway between a +Q and a -Q separated by distance d, draw or state the directions of the electric field vectors contributed by each charge and state whether the magnitudes add or cancel. What is the direction of the net field?

entry_ticket.expected_response: The force stays the same (unchanged). Algebraic reason: new F' = (1/4πε0) (q/2)(q'/2) / (r/2)^2 = (1/4πε0) q q' / r^2 = F.
entry_ticket.prompt: Two identical neutral spheres C and D are touched to charged spheres A and B respectively. Initially A has charge +q and B has charge +q'. After touching, symmetry makes the charges on A+C and B+D become +q/2 and +q'/2. If the centre-to-centre distance r between A and B is then halved (r → r/2), how does the magnitude of the electrostatic force between A and B compare to the original force F = (1/4πε0) q q' / r^2 ? Write one short sentence and a one-line algebraic reason.

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain, using atomic-scale evidence, why rubbing two neutral materials transfers electrons between them and does not create net charge. Keep your answer to three or four sentences.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Mentions that rubbing causes electrons to move from atoms in one material to atoms in the other due to different electron affinity/work function; states that electrons (not protons) move between surfaces; explains that charge is conserved so one object becomes negatively charged and the other positively charged by equal and opposite amounts; links this atomic transfer to macroscopic observation (e.g., one object gains net negative charge and the other equal net positive charge).

homework.submission_format: Written solutions (handwritten scanned or digital document with calculations and sketches).
tasks: Problem 1 (calculate, 20 minutes): Three point charges sit on the x-axis: +6.0 μC at x=0.00 m, -3.0 μC at x=0.40 m, and +2.0 μC at x=0.90 m. Find the net electric field vector (magnitude and sign along x) at x=0.60 m. Show the vector contributions from each charge, include units, and use k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2.

Problem 2 (sketch + explain, 10 minutes): Draw the electric field lines for an isolated electric dipole (a small +Q and -Q separated by a short distance). On your sketch, indicate direction of field lines, where line density is largest, and write one sentence explaining what line density means in terms of E-field strength.

Problem 3 (short written, 15 minutes): In 4–6 sentences, answer the exit-ticket question again: explain why rubbing transfers electrons and not protons, and why this process leaves no net charge created overall. Use the terms 'electron', 'ion', and 'conservation of charge'.

mentor_moment.story: You rub a balloon on your sweater and hold it near your hair; the hair stands up and the balloon sticks. Electrons moved from the sweater to the balloon, leaving the sweater slightly positive and the balloon negative.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Seeing hair stand up shows electrons moved between materials and that the two objects gained equal and opposite net charge — charge was transferred, not created.
mentor_moment.title: Balloon and Hair

anticipated_questions: Why do the neutral spheres split charge in half?
Is the test charge the same as the charged spheres?
Why did we let them touch—does that change total charge?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the entry-ticket algebra if a student offers it: F = (1/4πε0) q q' / r^2 and student claim F' = (1/4πε0) (q/2)(q'/2) / (r/2)^2 = ?
teacher_script.heading: Activate prior knowledge / Entry ticket review
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Collect quick responses (thumbs up for "same", thumbs down for "changes"). Ask one student to read their sentence aloud. If a student gives the "force increases by 4" answer, write that algebra on the board and say: "Hold that — we'll check it". Remind class: we already know Coulomb's law in vector form and that charge is quantised. Say the objective out loud: "Today we will use superposition to add forces, define electric field, and show the field superposes too. By the end you should be able to explain why rubbing transfers electrons rather than creating new net charge."

anticipated_questions: Do we need to use unit vectors every time?
What if the test charge is negative?
Does the presence of q change Q1 and Q2?
teacher_script.board_action: Draw two charges on horizontal line: label Q1 at -d, Q2 at +d, test charge q at 0. Write each force term as a vector using the provided Coulomb-like formula and then write total F = F1 + F2 (vector sum).
teacher_script.heading: Introduce principle of superposition for forces
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We will build the total force from two point charges by adding the vector forces from each. I will show this with a simple two-charge arrangement, then extend to many charges." Draw two fixed source charges Q1 at x = -d and Q2 at x = +d on the board (label magnitudes and signs; use Q1 = +2 μC and Q2 = -1 μC as a concrete example). Place a small test charge q at x = 0 (use q = +1 μC). Ask: "What is the force on q from Q1? From Q2?" Have students call out directions; then write each force using the Coulomb-like point-force expression: F_r = (1/4πε0)(Q q / r^2) r (point to directions). Emphasize vectors: show unit vectors from source to test charge, calculate magnitudes with distances (d and d). Then say: "Total force = vector sum of these individual forces" and write the sum. Point out this is the principle of superposition: add each vector contribution.

anticipated_questions: Why divide by q — what if q is not small?
Is E a physical thing or just a calculation?
If q is negative, do we still divide by q the same way?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the exact wording of the Test charge definition. Write E from a point charge as derived: E = (1/4πε0) Q / r^2 r (derive by dividing F_r by q). Show units: N/C. Then write E_net = E1 + E2 and plug numeric values for the example, showing arithmetic with units.
teacher_script.heading: Define electric field and its superposition
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Instead of talking about forces on a specific test charge, we define the electric field E that tells us the force per unit test charge at each point. Read the definition with me: 'Test charge: A charge q used to probe the electric field of a source charge; ideally negligibly small so it does not disturb the source charge distribution.'" Write the definition on the board. Then derive the field from the force: place the same Q1 and Q2 on the board and say: "Field from a single point source Q at distance r is E = F/q = (1/4πε0) Q / r^2 r. So the net field is the vector sum of fields from each charge." Emphasize units: show F in newtons (N), q in coulombs (C), so E in N/C. Use the earlier numeric example (Q1=+2 μC, Q2=-1 μC, point at x=0) and compute E1 and E2 numerically (carry units), then add vectors to get net E. Conclude: once we have E, any test charge q experiences F = q E. Finally state the superposition principle for E in words: "Net E = sum of E from each source charge."

anticipated_questions: Why is flux a scalar if it comes from a vector dot product?
What does 'density of lines' mean quantitatively?
What units does flux have—how do they relate to the equation?
teacher_script.board_action: Draw a positive charge with radial arrows; draw dipole sketch. Draw a little area element with normal, label θ. Write the electric flux element formula exactly as given and do the numeric calculation: ΔΦ = 100 N/C × 0.02 m^2 × cos60° = 1.0 N·m^2/C.
teacher_script.heading: Demonstration and guided practice: field lines and flux
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Now a quick demonstration with field lines and flux to connect the vector field to pictures and to area crossing." Draw a positive point charge and sketch radial arrows outward. Explain: "Electric field lines: curves whose tangent gives field direction; dense lines → stronger field; lines start on positive and end on negative charges." Ask a student to come up and draw lines for a positive-negative pair (dipole). Then introduce electric flux wording exactly: read: 'Electric flux: Scalar quantity through an area element ΔS given by the surface dot product E·ΔS = E ΔS cosθ; for a closed surface, area element direction is outward normal.' Show a small flat area element ΔS in the field and draw angle θ between E and normal. Calculate a numeric example: E = 100 N/C, ΔS = 0.02 m^2, θ = 60°, compute ΔΦ = E ΔS cosθ with units (N·m^2/C).

anticipated_questions: So charge isn't created when you rub—how do you show that experimentally?
If electrons move, can the objects end up with more overall net charge than before?
Do field lines actually exist or are they just a picture?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the algebraic check for the entry-ticket so it is clear. Then list three consolidation bullets: 1) Superposition (forces) — vector sum; 2) Electric field — characteristic of source charges, E = F/q (units N/C); 3) Flux element ΔΦ = E ΔS cosθ. Also write the test-charge and electric-flux definitions verbatim for students to copy.
teacher_script.heading: Check and consolidate: charge transfer and exit summary
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Return to the entry-ticket example. Recompute the algebra on board showing explicitly: F' = (1/4πε0) (q/2)(q'/2) / (r/2)^2 = (1/4πε0) q q' / r^2. Ask students to explain in one sentence why halving charges and halving distance cancel. Then pose the atomic-scale question to the class: "When two neutral materials are rubbed, why are electrons transferred rather than new charge created?" Prompt with these points to elicit: electrons are mobile, atoms lose or gain electrons, total net charge of system is conserved (electrons move from one object to the other), and protons remain bound in nuclei. Have students write one short answer on paper. Finish by summarising the three core points on the board: superposition for forces, field definition and superposition, and flux element.

bullet_points: Point charge (definition): charge concentrated at a point when size ≪ distances considered.
Test charge (definition): small probe charge that does not disturb source distribution.
Electric field (operational): E(r) = F(r) / q_test. Unit: N/C.
Coulomb-like point-force expression: F_r = (1/4πε0) (Q q / r^2) r̂
Electric field of a point charge: E(r) = (1/4πε0) (Q / r^2) r̂
Gauss's law (statement): Electric flux through closed surface = (enclosed charge)/ε0
Dipole: +q at z=+a, -q at z=-a (separation 2a). Dipole moment p = q(2a) directed from - to +.
Far-field (r ≫ a) axial result: E_axis = (1/4πε0) (2 p / r^3) (along axis from - to +).
Far-field (r ≫ a) equatorial result: E_equator = (1/4πε0) ( - p / r^3 ) (radially inward).
Note: Dipole far-field falls off as 1/r^3 because leading 1/r^2 terms cancel between the two charges.
Force on test charge: F = q_test E
diagrams_to_draw: 1D sketch: +Q at x=0, +q at x=2 cm, +Q at x=4 cm with equal opposite force arrows on +q.
2D coordinate sketch: Q at (0,0), q at (0.30,0.40) m with vector r⃗ drawn and components labeled; show r̂=(0.6,0.8).
Dipole on z-axis: -q at z=-a, +q at z=+a, field point at z=r on axis; show distances r-a and r+a.
Dipole equatorial sketch: field point at distance r in midplane; show vector contributions from +q and -q and resultant.
headings: Point-charge field and Coulomb force (vector form)

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Compute displacement from q to Q: r = r1 - r2 = (0.02, -0.03, 0) m. Distance r = sqrt(0.02^2+(-0.03)^2)=0.03606 m. Unit vector r̂ = (0.02/0.03606, -0.03/0.03606, 0) ≈ (0.5547, -0.83205, 0). Coulomb magnitude: k|Qq|/r^2 where k=1/(4πϵ0)≈8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2. |F| = 8.99×10^9*(3.0×10^-6)*(1.0×10^-6)/(0.03606^2) ≈ 20.7 N. Sign: Q is positive, q negative → attractive, so force on q points toward Q, i.e. +r̂. Vector force F ≈ 20.7 N * (0.5547, -0.83205, 0) ≈ (11.5, -17.2, 0) N.
checkpoint_questions.question: Two point charges, Q = +3.0 μC at position r1 = (0.02 m, 0, 0) and q = -1.0 μC at r2 = (0, 0.03 m, 0). Write the vector expression (magnitude and direction) for the Coulomb force on q due to Q using Coulomb's law in vector form.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Electric field E at a point is defined as the force per unit test charge: E = F/q (operationally measured by placing a small test charge and measuring force). SI unit: newtons per coulomb (N/C). Relation: F = q E. (State that the test charge should be negligibly small so it doesn't disturb the source.)
checkpoint_questions.question: State the operational definition of the electric field at a point and give its SI unit. Then, using that definition, write the relation between force and field for a test charge q placed at that point.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Start with sum of two point-charge fields on the axis: E = (1/4πϵ0)[ q/(r-a)^2 - q/(r+a)^2 ] (along x̂). Combine fractions to get numerator ≈ q[ (r+a)^2 - (r-a)^2 ] / (r^2 - a^2)^2 = q(4ar) / (r^4) to leading order. Use r >> a to approximate (r±a)^2 ≈ r^2 ± 2ar and denominators ≈ r^4 (binomial/Taylor expansion neglecting terms O((a/r)^2)). Result E ≈ (1/4πϵ0)(4aq / r^3) x̂ = (1/4πϵ0)(2p / r^3) x̂ since dipole moment p = q(2a) directed along +x. This shows E ∝ p / r^3; note signs depend on axis side.
checkpoint_questions.question: For a dipole consisting of +q at x = +a and −q at x = −a, sketch the algebraic steps (no long algebra) that lead to the far-field (r >> a) dependence E ∝ p / r^3 along the axis. Identify where a binomial/taylor approximation is used and how p appears.

entry_ticket.expected_response: Sketch: arrows from each source pointing away from each +Q. The arrows from the two +Q's point in opposite directions at the test charge and have equal magnitude, so they cancel. Net force = zero. Short reason: the distances to each +Q are equal so Coulomb forces are equal and opposite.
entry_ticket.prompt: Two point charges, +Q at x = 0 and +Q at x = 4 cm. A test charge +q is placed at x = 2 cm. Draw the direction of the net electric force on +q and say whether the magnitude is zero, nonzero but small, or large. (A sketch and one sentence.)

exit_ticket.prompt: A small dipole has charges +2.0 μC at x = +0.005 m and −2.0 μC at x = −0.005 m. Estimate the magnitude and direction of the electric field at a point on the +x axis at x = 0.20 m using the far-field dipole formula. Show the key step that yields the 1/r^3 dependence and express your answer in N/C.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Student computes dipole moment p = q(2a) = (2.0×10^-6 C)(0.01 m) = 2.0×10^-8 C·m, uses E_axis ≈ (1/4πϵ0)(2p / r^3) with r = 0.20 m and k=8.99×10^9, evaluates E ≈ (8.99×10^9)(2×2.0×10^-8)/(0.20^3) ≈ numerical value ≈ 8.99×10^9 *4.0×10^-8 / 0.008 = (8.99×10^9 *5.0×10^-6) ≈ 45 N/C, and states direction is +x (away from dipole if appropriate). Work shows 1/r^3 step and units N/C.

homework.submission_format: Handwritten solutions scanned or photographed and uploaded as a single PDF; each problem must show units and intermediate steps.
tasks: Problem 1 (20 min): Two point charges +5.0 μC at (0,0,0) and −3.0 μC at (0.04 m, 0, 0). Calculate the vector electric field at the point (0.02 m, 0.03 m, 0). Show displacement vectors, magnitudes, unit vectors, and final vector in N/C.

Problem 2 (25 min): Derive the far-field electric field (leading term only) on the perpendicular bisector (equatorial plane) of a dipole with charges +q at +a and −q at −a. Show the algebra where terms cancel to give E = −(1/4πϵ0)(p / r^3) in direction.

Problem 3 (15 min): Using Gauss's law, explain in one paragraph why the electric field inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell is zero. Reference the Gaussian surface and enclosed charge explicitly.

mentor_moment.story: In a lab, a student used a too-large test charge and got a different field than theory predicted; after switching to a much smaller probe charge, the measured force matched the calculated E·q. The group realized the probe must be negligible.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Always use (or imagine) a test charge small enough that it doesn't change the source distribution; E is defined as force per unit charge.
mentor_moment.title: Lab probe surprise

anticipated_questions: Why do we treat the charges as points instead of small spheres? (Answer: point charge means size ≪ distances considered.)
Does the sign of the test charge always matter? (Answer: it changes direction of each force but not whether magnitudes cancel in this symmetric case.)
Is electric field the same as force? (Answer: field is force per unit test charge; we'll state unit N/C.)
teacher_script.board_action: Display the same 1D sketch: x-axis, +Q at 0, +q at 2 cm, +Q at 4 cm. Draw two force arrows on +q: one right, one left, equal length. Label distances 2 cm and 2 cm. Write one-sentence conclusion: Net force = 0.
teacher_script.heading: Activate prior knowledge — discuss entry ticket
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Look up here. Five students read your sketch and sentence aloud quickly. Who answered 'zero' for the net force? Who answered 'nonzero'?" Wait for a show of hands. Then say: "Good. One quick reason: for the arrangement +Q at 0 and +Q at 4 cm with +q at 2 cm, why would forces cancel? Who can point to the two forces on the sketch and say which way each arrow points?" If no one volunteers, point yourself: "The force from the left +Q on +q pushes right; from the right +Q it pushes left. Distances are equal so magnitudes are equal. So net force is zero." Then ask: "If the test charge had been -q at 2 cm, what would the net force be?" Wait for responses and correct: "It would also be zero because the magnitudes still match and the directions both point toward the positive sources, producing equal and opposite forces."

anticipated_questions: Why did we pick r̂ from Q to q instead of q to Q? (Answer: be consistent; formula as written uses r̂ from source to field point; sign of scalar product captures attraction/repulsion.)
Where did the minus sign come from? (Answer: it comes from q being negative so product Qq is negative.)
Do units check out? (Answer: yes — show N from the numbers; 1/4πε0 has units N·m^2/C^2 so after multiplying charges and dividing by m^2 gives N.)
What if charges are both positive? (Answer: product positive → force along +r̂ → repulsive.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write data: Q=+2.0 μC at (0,0); q=-1.0 μC at (0.30,0.40) m. Write r_vec = (0.30,0.40) m, r = 0.50 m, r̂=(0.6,0.8). Write formula F = (1/4πε0) (Q q / r^2) r̂. Show numeric steps and final vector F = (-0.043, -0.058) N.
teacher_script.heading: Demonstration + guided vector Coulomb example
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We'll apply Coulomb's law in vector form to a quick 2D example." Draw on board: point charge Q = +2.0 μC at r1 = (0.00 m, 0.00 m) and point charge q = -1.0 μC at r2 = (0.30 m, 0.40 m). Ask: "What is the vector from Q to q, and the separation r?" Wait for student replies and then compute aloud: r_vec = r2 - r1 = (0.30, 0.40) m. Say: "Compute its magnitude: r = sqrt(0.30^2+0.40^2) = 0.50 m. Unit vector r̂ = (0.30,0.40)/0.50 = (0.6,0.8)." Next write Coulomb-like point-force expression and apply numbers step by step: F = (1/4πε0) Q q / r^2 r̂. Use (1/4πε0)=9.0×10^9 N·m^2/C^2. Compute scalar factor: 9.0e9*(2.0e-6 * -1.0e-6)/(0.50^2) = compute aloud: numerator 9.0e9 * -2.0e-12 = -1.8e-2 N·m^2 / (0.25 m^2) = -7.2e-2 N. Then multiply by r̂ = (0.6,0.8): F = (-0.072)*(0.6,0.8) N = (-0.043, -0.058) N. Say: "Interpretation: negative sign means force points opposite our chosen r̂ (i.e. toward the source), consistent with an attractive force because q is negative and Q positive." Ask: "Which component is larger in magnitude, x or y? Do the signs make sense with the sketch?"

anticipated_questions: Why can we expand 1/(r±a)^2? (Answer: because r ≫ a, so a/r is small; use binomial expansion to first order.)
Is p = q·2a always? (Answer: for this symmetric dipole yes; generally p = q·d where d is vector from negative to positive charge.)
Why does the field fall like 1/r^3 instead of 1/r^2? (Answer: cancellation of leading 1/r^2 terms from the two opposite charges leaves next-order 1/r^3 term.)
What about directions off-axis? (Answer: those require vector addition; we showed axis and equatorial plane which are the canonical results.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw dipole on z-axis: -q at -a, +q at +a, field point on +z axis at r. Write the point-charge field formula at top. Write expansions: 1/(r±a)^2 ≈ 1/r^2(1 ∓ 2a/r). Show subtraction leading to E_axis ≈ (1/4πε0)(2qa/r^3). Then write p = q(2a) and E_axis = (1/4πε0)(2p/r^3). Also draw equatorial sketch and final result E_equator = (1/4πε0)(-p/r^3) (radially).
teacher_script.heading: Teacher-led derivation: dipole far-field (start)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Now we derive the far-field of a simple dipole and show the 1/r^3 dependence. We'll use a dipole of +q at z = +a and -q at z = -a on the z-axis. Our field point is at distance r from the origin with r ≫ a. We'll get the field along the axis first, then the equatorial plane." Draw the dipole: +q at z=+a, -q at z=-a, field point on +z axis at z=r. Ask: "Write the field from each point charge using the point-charge field formula." Write E_+ = (1/4πε0) q (r - r_+)/|r - r_+|^3 and E_- similarly; but for axis we can use magnitudes: distance from +q to field point is r - a; from -q is r + a. Then expand for r ≫ a: 1/(r - a)^2 ≈ 1/r^2 * (1 + 2a/r) and 1/(r + a)^2 ≈ 1/r^2 * (1 - 2a/r) (explain: use binomial expansion to first order). Substitute and take differences to get net E along axis: E ≈ (1/4πε0) (2qa / r^3) in +z direction. Define dipole moment p = q(2a) ? Wait — correct definition: p = q (2a) if using +q and -q separated by 2a along axis; but more standard is p = q * (2a) in direction from - to +. Say: "We express result in terms of p: E_axis = (1/4πε0) (2p / r^3) in the +z direction." Emphasize units: p has units C·m, so the combination gives N/C. Then repeat quickly for equatorial point (on plane at distance r from origin, at midplane): contributions are opposite and give E = -(1/4πε0) (p / r^3) radially inward. Show sign reasoning: along equator, fields from +q and -q have components that cancel along z and add radially inward with net magnitude p/r^3.

anticipated_questions: Why is equatorial magnitude half the axial? (Answer: derivation gives factor 2 difference; axis is 2p/r^3, equator is -p/r^3.)
Are these numbers realistic? (Answer: yes; field strengths depend on q and separation; units N/C used.)
Why multiply by test charge to get force? (Answer: F = q_test E; that's the operational definition.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write tasks A and B text. Show numeric steps for p = 4.0e-8 C·m. Show calculation lines for E_axis and E_equator and final numeric answers: E_axis = +720 N/C, E_equator = -360 N/C (radial inward). Write F_on_test = q_test * E as reminder.
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice: quick calculations and interpretation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Hand out or display two short tasks to do in pairs for 6 minutes. Task A: A dipole with +q = 2.0×10^-6 C at +0.01 m and -q at -0.01 m. Find E on axis at r = 1.0 m using E_axis = (1/4πε0)(2p/r^3). Compute p and numeric E and state units. Task B: For same dipole, at equator r = 1.0 m, compute E_equator = (1/4πε0)(-p/r^3) and compare magnitude to axis value. Circulate, check arithmetic: p = q(2a)=2.0e-6*(0.02)=4.0e-8 C·m. Then scalar factor: 1/4πε0 = 9.0e9. For r=1.0 m, E_axis = 9.0e9*(2*4.0e-8)/(1^3)=9.0e9*(8.0e-8)=0.72×10^2? Compute carefully with students to reach E_axis = 720 N/C along +z. E_equator magnitude = half that = 360 N/C inward. Ask: "Which direction would a test charge +1.0 μC experience force?" Expect: F = q_test E, so 1.0e-6 C * E, numerically small in N.

anticipated_questions: If flux is zero, does that mean no field inside? (Answer: no — flux zero means net through closed surface is zero; fields can enter and leave.)
Does 1/r^3 apply near the dipole? (Answer: no — it's the far-field approximation for r ≫ a.)
Will we need the binomial expansion formula? (Answer: yes briefly for derivations; you'll be shown how it's used to first order.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write two quick check questions and answers: 1) r→2r ⇒ E→E/8. 2) Dipole inside closed surface with net charge 0 ⇒ Φ = 0. Write operational definition: E = F/q, unit N/C. Underline 'useful for torque and Gauss law symmetry next.'
teacher_script.heading: Formative check + consolidation and link forward
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Give two quick oral questions and have students signal answers with thumbs: 1) "If we double r, how does the dipole field at far-field change?" (Expected: decreases by 8, because 1/r^3). 2) "Does Gauss's law still hold for a dipole inside a closed surface that encloses no net charge? What is the net flux?" (Expected: flux = 0 because net enclosed charge is zero.) Then say: "Write down the operational definition of electric field and its unit: E = F/q, unit N/C. Tomorrow we'll use torque on a dipole in a uniform E and more Gauss law symmetry problems."

bullet_points: Superposition: Net force on a charge = vector sum of forces from each other charge (each pairwise force is unchanged by others).
Coulomb's law used per pair: F = k q_test q_i / r^2  (use vector direction; k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2).
Compute magnitudes: F_i = k·(0.5×10^-6 C)·(q_i)/(r_i^2) ; assign sign: right = +x, left = -x ; net F = Σ F_i (with signs) → result in N.
Dipole: p = q s  (from negative to positive). Forces on +q and -q in uniform E cancel: F_net = 0, but produce torque.
Torque on electric dipole: τ = p × E  (units: C·m × N/C = N·m).
Definitions (exact wording): σ = ΔQ/ΔS  (surface charge density), unit: C·m^-2.
λ = ΔQ/Δl  (linear charge density), unit: C·m^-1.
ρ = ΔQ/ΔV  (volume charge density), unit: C·m^-3.
Small flux element: ΔΦ = E · ΔS  (ΔS is area vector).
Gauss's law (integral, closed surface): ∮_S E · dS = q_enc / ε_0
diagrams_to_draw: Number line showing q1 at -0.10 m, q2 at 0, q3 at +0.10 m, q0 at +0.05 m with arrows showing individual forces on q0.
Dipole cartoon: -q and +q separated by vector s, centre marked, r+ and r- vectors, uniform E shown as parallel upward arrows, show F+ and F- and torque sense (curved arrow).
Small area element ΔS with normal vector and field vector E showing dot product for ΔΦ = E · ΔS.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Compute force from q1 on q3: F13 = k q1 q3 / r13^2 to the right (positive x) because both positive. r13 = 0.35-0.20 = 0.15 m. k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2. F13 = (8.99×10^9)(3.0×10^-6)(1.0×10^-6)/(0.15^2) ≈ 1.20 N to the +x. Force from q2 on q3: F23 = k q2 q3 / r23^2; q2 is negative so attract — direction to the +x if q2 is to right of q3? Here q2 at 0.50 m, q3 at 0.35 m, so attraction is to the +x. r23 = 0.50-0.35 = 0.15 m. Magnitude F23 = (8.99×10^9)(2.0×10^-6)(1.0×10^-6)/(0.15^2) ≈ 0.80 N to the +x. Net F = F13 + F23 = 1.20 N + 0.80 N = 2.00 N in +x direction. Teacher can mark correct units (N), correct use of k, and correct signs/directions.
checkpoint_questions.question: Two point charges lie on the x-axis: q1 = +3.0 μC at x = 0.20 m and q2 = -2.0 μC at x = 0.50 m. A test charge q3 = +1.0 μC is at x = 0.35 m. Using superposition, find the net electrostatic force on q3 (give magnitude, sign, and units). Show the vector (one-dimensional) addition and the electric constant you use.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: λ (linear charge density) = ΔQ/Δl, unit C·m^-1. Example: a 2.0 m wire carrying total charge +6.0 μC has average λ = 6.0×10^-6 C / 2.0 m = 3.0×10^-6 C·m^-1. σ (surface charge density) = ΔQ/ΔS, unit C·m^-2. Example: a square metal plate 0.10 m × 0.10 m carrying −1.0 μC has σ = −1.0×10^-6 C / 0.01 m^2 = −1.0×10^-4 C·m^-2. ρ (volume charge density) = ΔQ/ΔV, unit C·m^-3. Example: a small sphere of volume 4.0×10^-6 m^3 with total charge +2.0 μC has ρ = 2.0×10^-6 C / 4.0×10^-6 m^3 = 0.50 C·m^-3. Teacher checks for correct formulas, units, and plausible numeric examples.
checkpoint_questions.question: Write the macroscopic definitions and SI units for linear, surface, and volume charge densities (λ, σ, ρ). For each, give a concrete physical example (one sentence) with numbers and units.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: (a) Torque magnitude τ = p E sinθ. τ = (4.0×10^-29 C·m)(2.0×10^5 N·C^-1)sin60° = (8.0×10^-24 N·m)(√3/2) ≈ 6.9×10^-24 N·m. Units N·m. (b) In a uniform field the net force is zero because equal and opposite forces on the + and − charges sum to zero; only a torque acts. Teacher checks numerical value with units and the short explanation that uniform E gives no net force.
checkpoint_questions.question: A permanent electric dipole with dipole moment p = 4.0×10^-29 C·m is placed in a uniform electric field E = 2.0×10^5 N·C^-1. The angle between p and E is 60°. (a) What is the magnitude of the torque on the dipole? (b) Does the dipole experience a net force? Explain in one sentence.

entry_ticket.expected_response: Direction: to the right (positive x). Why: the closer +2.0 μC at +10 cm pulls q0 to the right more strongly than the +2.0 μC at -10 cm pulls to the left, and the +1.0 μC at 0 cm pulls left but weaker.
entry_ticket.prompt: You have three point charges on a line: q1 = +2.0 μC at x = -10 cm, q2 = +1.0 μC at x = 0 cm, q3 = +2.0 μC at x = +10 cm. A small test charge q0 = +0.5 μC is placed at x = 5 cm. In one short sentence, write the direction of the net electrostatic force on q0 and WHY (no calculation needed).

exit_ticket.prompt: A charge qA = +4.0 μC sits at (0, 0) m and qB = −1.0 μC sits at (0.30, 0) m. A third charge qC = +2.0 μC is at (0.30, 0.40) m. (1) Using vector superposition and k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2, calculate the net electrostatic force vector on qC (give components in N). Show the two force vectors you add. (2) Write the formula and SI unit for surface charge density σ.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Correct computation of the two force vectors (from qA and qB) with direction and components, correct use of distances (include √(0.30^2+0.40^2) where needed), numeric addition giving net Fx and Fy in newtons with k shown; and correct definition σ = ΔQ/ΔS with units C·m^-2.

homework.submission_format: Handwritten solutions with calculations shown; box final numeric answers with units on each task.
tasks: Compute the net force on a +1.0 μC charge located at the origin from three charges at (0.10 m, 0), (−0.10 m, 0), and (0, 0.15 m). Use k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2. Show vector components and final magnitude and direction (degrees).

A thin insulating rod 0.50 m long carries total charge +9.0 μC uniformly distributed. (a) Compute the linear charge density λ and give its unit. (b) If you take a 0.10 m piece of the rod, what charge does that piece carry? Show units.

Sketch a small diagram and explain in two sentences why a permanent dipole in a strictly uniform electric field feels a torque but no net force. Reference the forces on the positive and negative charges and show how they add.

mentor_moment.story: In a lab, my partner and I measured forces between three charged beads. We first added magnitudes and got nonsense; only when we added vectors component-wise did the balance of forces make sense and the beads stayed where predicted.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Always resolve electrostatic forces into components and add those components — correct directions matter as much as magnitudes.
mentor_moment.title: Lab day surprise: vector addition matters

anticipated_questions: Do we have to include the test charge's own field? (No, we consider forces on q0 from the other charges.)
Should we use Coulomb's constant explicitly? (Yes — we'll carry k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2 if we calculate.)
What if the charges were negative? (Direction would reverse for that pull; we'll use sign in vector addition.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the numerical positions and charges from the prompt on the board in a simple line sketch.
teacher_script.heading: Collect entry tickets & quick share
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Ask students to hand entry tickets to the edge of their desk. Read one aloud: "q1 = +2 μC at -10 cm, q2 = +1 μC at 0, q3 = +2 μC at +10 cm, test q0 = +0.5 μC at +5 cm. Which way is the net force on q0?" Then say: "Don't calculate yet — just say direction and why." Call on 2 volunteers who answered differently. If a volunteer says 'left' ask: "Which charge gives the biggest pull on q0? How does distance matter?" If they say 'right' ask: "Which two pulls oppose each other?" Conclude: "Most of you said right because the nearer +2 μC at +10 cm dominates. We'll see how to get that answer quantitatively using superposition."

anticipated_questions: Do we need vector components here? (Yes if not collinear; here all are on x so we use sign convention.)
Why can we add forces linearly? (Because superposition says contributions are independent.)
Do we include forces between the other charges? (Not for the net force on q0; only forces on q0 from each other charge.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write stepwise Coulomb magnitudes with numbers substituted and carry units; at the end write the net force numerically with units and a +x or -x sign.
teacher_script.heading: Introduce and state superposition principle
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Superposition: the net force on a charge from several other charges is the vector sum of the forces from each one; other charges don't change each pairwise force." Write the formula-free statement on board. Then do a short worked example step-by-step without pre-calculation: use the entry-ticket configuration. Say: "Let's compute the force on q0 from each charge and add them as vectors. We'll use Coulomb's law for each pair: F = k q0 q / r^2 and direction along the line between charges." Write k and units on the board. Calculate aloud and on the board: For q2 at 0 cm: r = 5 cm = 0.05 m, F2 = k*(0.5e-6 C)*(1.0e-6 C)/(0.05^2). For q3 at +10 cm: r = 0.05 m, F3 = k*(0.5e-6)*(2.0e-6)/(0.05^2). For q1 at -10 cm: r = 0.15 m, F1 = k*(0.5e-6)*(2.0e-6)/(0.15^2). Evaluate each magnitude using k = 8.99×10^9 and show arithmetic steps, carrying units N. Then assign signs: right = +x, left = -x. Add F = F3 + F2(-) + F1(-) with their signs to get net. Point out which term dominated. Ask students to check arithmetic in pairs for 2 minutes.

anticipated_questions: Why is p defined from negative to positive? (By convention, so sign of p encodes orientation.)
How can forces cancel but a torque remain? (Because forces act at different positions producing a net moment.)
If the field is non-uniform, will there be a net force? (Yes — briefly acknowledge and promise a later example.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw dipole cartoon: two charges separated by vector s, show r+ and r- from centre, write F+ and F-, show cross-product algebra leading to τ = p × E and label units.
teacher_script.heading: Demonstration: dipole torque derivation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Now we derive the torque on a dipole in a uniform field. I'll use a simple permanent dipole: +q and -q separated by distance d, with the dipole centred at origin and the vector from -q to +q called s. The dipole moment is p = q s (direction from negative to positive)." Draw the two charges and label forces from a uniform E field pointing up. Then calculate the forces: top charge feels F = qE upward (if +q) or downward (if -q) — be explicit: the +q feels F+ = q E, the -q feels F- = -q E. Show that net force F+ + F- = 0. Next compute torque about the centre: write τ = r+ × F+ + r- × F-. Show algebra that simplifies to τ = p × E. Keep units: p in C·m, E in N/C so τ in N·m. Point at the written final formula (use the source formula exactly). Then ask: "If E is uniform there is no net force — what if E varies across the dipole?" (briefly note there can be net force — we do not derive that now.)

anticipated_questions: Why are the deltas used instead of limits? (We use macroscopic averages; later we'll take limits to define continuous densities.)
Are units always C/m^n? (Yes: length power matches dimension.)
Does ΔS have direction? (Yes: ΔS is a vector normal to the area; that's why we use the dot product.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the three density definitions with units and write ΔΦ = E · ΔS and the Gauss's law formula exactly as given in the source.
teacher_script.heading: Introduce continuous charge densities (λ, σ, ρ) and electric flux element
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "When charge is spread out, we define densities: linear λ, surface σ, volume ρ as charge per length, area, volume. We'll use the exact wording from the text." Read and write each definition exactly: σ = ΔQ/ΔS, λ = ΔQ/Δl, ρ = ΔQ/ΔV. For each, state SI units aloud and write them: λ in C·m^-1, σ in C·m^-2, ρ in C·m^-3. Then introduce electric flux for a small area: ΔΦ = E · ΔS and say the flux through a closed surface sums to q_enc/ε0 — write Gauss's law (integral form) on the board and read it aloud, naming ε0 units C^2/(N·m^2) if asked. Give a quick physical anchor: "If a small area faces the field, E·ΔS equals how many field lines pierce that area weighted by strength."

anticipated_questions: Do we round constants? (Use the given numbers; keep units consistent.)
For the cube, do we use m^3 for volume? (Yes — convert cm to m before computing.)
What if distribution isn't uniform? (Then λ, σ, ρ vary with position; these formulas give local/average values.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write each prompt and then write the computed λ, σ, ρ with units after students report.
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice: identify densities and compute ΔQ
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Project or draw three small quick prompts and read them one at a time. Prompt A: "A thin wire has total charge Q = 6.0×10^-6 C uniformly distributed along length L = 2.0 m. What is λ and its unit?" Prompt B: "A square metal plate 0.10 m by 0.10 m has total charge Q = 1.0×10^-8 C uniformly on its surface. What is σ?" Prompt C: "A small cube of insulating material of side 2.0 cm contains total charge Q = 4.0×10^-9 C uniformly. What is ρ?" For each, give students 90 seconds to compute in pairs, then call a pair to report and write results on the board. Insist on units written explicitly. Walk around and check one or two groups, correcting arithmetic if needed.

anticipated_questions: Will we need long algebra for wire/plane examples? (We'll keep symmetry to make integrals simple.)
Can you show the dipole torque again? (Offer to re-draw after class if needed.)
teacher_script.board_action: Underline the key final results on the board: superposition statement, definitions, Gauss's law, τ = p × E.
teacher_script.heading: Quick check & consolidation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Ask three rapid oral questions and have students thumb-signal (1 = A, 2 = B, 3 = C) to show answers. Q1: "If two equal positive charges are equidistant from a test charge, will their pulls cancel?" Q2: "Unit of surface charge density σ?" Q3: "Does a dipole in a uniform field experience net force or net torque or both?" After each thumbs, call on a student to justify briefly (one sentence). Close: "Next time we'll use these ideas to compute fields of an infinite wire and plane; today we made superposition and densities concrete."

bullet_points: Use Gauss's law: ∮ E·dA = Qenc/ε0
Choose Gaussian surface by symmetry; carry units through every step
Infinite wire: cylindrical surface, radius r, length L → Qenc = λL
Infinite plane: pillbox area A → Qenc = σA
Spherical shell: spherical surface radius r → Qenc = q for r>R, Qenc = 0 for r<R
diagrams_to_draw: Cylindrical Gaussian surface around a straight wire: label radius r and length L; show E arrows radially outward on curved surface and perpendicular to end caps
Pillbox straddling an infinite plane: draw top and bottom faces area A, show E arrows perpendicular on both sides
Spherical shell with two Gaussian surfaces: one r>R, one r<R; show radial E arrows outside and none inside

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Symmetry: field is radial and constant on curved surface. Gaussian surface area = (2π r L). Gauss's law: ∮E·dA = E(2π r L) = Q_enc/ε0. Enclosed charge Q_enc = λ L. So E(2π r L) = λ L/ε0 → E(r) = λ/(2π ε0 r). Units: λ in C/m, ε0 in C^2/(N·m^2), r in m → E in N/C (or V/m).
checkpoint_questions.question: You choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L around an infinitely long straight wire with uniform linear charge density λ. Write the Gauss law integral and show how you get the magnitude of the electric field E(r) at the curved surface. (Answer in symbols; state units for each quantity briefly.)

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Gaussian pillbox has two flat faces area A, one on each side of plane. Field normal to plane and constant on faces. Flux = E·A + E·A = 2EA. Enclosed charge = σ A. Gauss: 2EA = σ A/ε0 → E = σ/(2ε0). Field is constant with distance because plane is infinite: symmetry means no preferred distance and field lines are straight and normal, so E doesn't vary with r.
checkpoint_questions.question: Sketch a Gaussian pillbox that straddles an infinite charged plane with surface charge density σ. Use Gauss's law to find the magnitude of the electric field on one side of the plane. Explain why the field does not depend on distance from the plane.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: For r<R: choose spherical Gaussian surface radius r. Enclosed charge = 0 (shell outside the surface) → ∮E·dA = 0 → E = 0 (N/C). For r>R: choose radius r. Enclosed charge = q → E(4π r^2) = q/ε0 → E(r) = q/(4π ε0 r^2) radial outward. Units: q in C, r in m, ε0 in C^2/(N·m^2) → E in N/C.
checkpoint_questions.question: For a thin spherical shell of radius R carrying total charge q, pick Gaussian surfaces for r<R and r>R and state the enclosed charge in each case. From that, write E(r) for both regions and state the physical units.

entry_ticket.expected_response: Students should circle B and write: "B has r in it so the field decreases with distance; A has no r so it can't depend on distance. For r=0.10 m, B gives a number with units N/C."
entry_ticket.prompt:
You have a long straight wire with uniform linear charge density λ = +2.0×10⁻⁶ C/m. At a point 0.10 m from the wire you measure the electric field to point radially outward. Which of these two expressions could be the magnitude of that field? Circle one and quickly write one sentence explaining your choice.

A) E = λ/(2ε0) 
B) E = λ/(2π ε0 r)

(Answer in 3 minutes.)

exit_ticket.prompt: A long charged wire has λ = 5.0×10^-8 C/m. A parallel infinite charged plane has σ = 8.85×10^-12 C/m^2. A thin spherical shell of radius 0.50 m carries total charge q = 2.0×10^-6 C. For each object, write the expression for the electric field magnitude at the following points and compute its numerical value (show units): (a) at r = 0.10 m from the wire axis, (b) at 0.20 m on one side of the plane, (c) at r = 0.25 m (inside) and r = 1.0 m (outside) the spherical shell.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Student submits a short answer with four items: (a) E_wire = λ/(2π ε0 r) and numerical value ≈ 5.0e-8/(2π·8.85e-12·0.10) ≈ 9.0×10^3 N/C (radial); (b) E_plane = σ/(2ε0) and numerical value ≈ 8.85e-12/(2·8.85e-12) = 0.5 N/C (normal); (c1) E_inside_shell (r=0.25 m) = 0 N/C; (c2) E_outside_shell (r=1.0 m) = q/(4π ε0 r^2) and numerical value ≈ 2.0e-6/(4π·8.85e-12·1.0^2) ≈ 1.8×10^5 N/C, with units N/C. (Numbers may vary slightly with rounding.)

homework.submission_format: Hand in one-page written solutions with steps and unit annotations; include numerical answers rounded to 2 significant figures where appropriate.
tasks: Derive the electric field of an infinite line charge using Gauss's law, but this time show every algebra step for solving E(r) from E(2π r L) = λ L/ε0; write units at each step. (10 minutes)

A pair-problem: Two infinite parallel planes carry equal and opposite surface charge densities σ and -σ. Sketch field lines and use superposition of the single-plane result to write E in the three regions (left of both, between, right of both). Give numerical answers for σ = 4.0×10^-9 C/m^2. (15 minutes)

Calculate the work (in joules) required to bring a 1.0 μC test charge from r = 2.0 m to r = 0.75 m outside the charged spherical shell (q = 2.0×10^-6 C, R = 0.5 m). Use the shell's outside-field expression. Show units in each line. (20 minutes)

mentor_moment.story: A student once tried to integrate Coulomb's law over a long wire point-by-point for hours; after we recognized cylindrical symmetry and used Gauss's law, the answer took five minutes.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Before you start heavy integration, ask: what symmetry can let Gauss's law or simple geometry do the work?
mentor_moment.title: Seeing symmetry save time

anticipated_questions: Why would anyone pick A? (students noticing A has no r)
Do we need to plug numbers in now?
What does ε0 mean again?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the day's objectives and the three target charge geometries: infinite wire (λ), infinite plane (σ), thin spherical shell (q).
teacher_script.heading: Collect entry tickets; set goal
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Turn to me when the 3 minutes are up. Collect one sentence answers from three different students: one who chose A, one who chose B, and one explanation that mentioned distance. Say: "Today we will use Gauss's law to derive the formulas you just guessed at. By the end you must be able to show the steps and explain the units. Keep your calculators handy; carry units through each calculation."

anticipated_questions: Why ignore the end caps? (students about field direction)
What if the wire isn't infinite? (edge effects)
Do we have to pick L? (it cancels)
teacher_script.board_action: Write: Assume cylinder radius r, length L. Then Flux = E(r)·(2π r L). Qenc = λ L. Gauss: E(2π r L) = λ L/ε0 → E(r) = λ/(2π ε0 r) n̂. Show numeric example substitution and final N/C value.
teacher_script.heading: Derive field of infinite straight wire
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We start with an infinitely long straight wire with uniform linear charge density λ (C/m). Choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface coaxial with the wire of radius r and length L. Ask: 'What symmetry tells us about the direction of E and its dependence on position around the cylinder?' Wait for 'radial, same at every point on the curved surface.' Then write Gauss's law on the board: ∮ E·dA = Qenc/ε0. Point to the curved side: 'Only the curved side contributes because on the end caps E is parallel to the axis and flux is zero if wire is along the axis.' Compute flux: E(r) × (curved surface area) = E(r) × (2π r L). Compute enclosed charge: Qenc = λ L. Solve for E(r): E(r) = λ/(2π ε0 r). Emphasize units: λ in C/m, r in m, ε0 in C²/(N·m²) so E in N/C. Draw example: λ = 2.0×10⁻⁶ C/m at r=0.10 m and compute E numerically: E = (2.0×10⁻⁶)/(2π×8.85×10⁻¹²×0.10) N/C; work the arithmetic on the board and give the value. Ask: 'Which direction is the vector?' and answer: radially outward (unit vector n̂).

anticipated_questions: Why does the field not depend on distance? (students surprised)
What about near the edge of a finite sheet? (edge effects)
Does thickness matter? (if thin sheet vs slab)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw the plane and pillbox. Write: Flux = 2EA. Qenc = σA. 2EA = σA/ε0 → E = σ/(2ε0) n̂ (direction ± depending on sign of σ).
teacher_script.heading: Derive field of infinite plane sheet
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Now an infinite planar sheet with uniform surface charge density σ (C/m²). Use a small cylindrical pillbox Gaussian surface that intersects the plane: one flat face above the plane, one below. Ask: 'What is the field direction and how does symmetry help?' Guide to answer: field is perpendicular to the plane and same magnitude on both sides. Write Gauss's law: ∮ E·dA = Qenc/ε0. The flux is E · A (top) + E · A (bottom) = 2 E A because field is normal and same magnitude on both sides. Enclosed charge is σ A (charge on the patch of plane inside the pillbox). So 2 E A = σ A/ε0 → E = σ/(2ε0). Emphasize units: σ in C/m² gives E in N/C. Ask: 'What changes if σ is negative?' Students should say 'direction reverses but magnitude same.'

anticipated_questions: Why is there no enclosed charge for r<R if shell has charge? (students clarifying 'thin shell' assumption)
Does this work if charge is not uniform? (only by symmetry)
What about inside a solid charged sphere? (not covered here)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw sphere and two Gaussian radii r>R and r<R. Write: For r>R: E(4π r²)=q/ε0 → E = q/(4π ε0 r²) r̂. For r<R: Qenc=0 → E=0.
teacher_script.heading: Derive field of a thin spherical shell (inside and outside)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Finally, a thin spherical shell of radius R carrying total charge q uniformly. Use a spherical Gaussian surface of radius r centered on the shell. Ask: 'What is E's direction and dependence on angle?' Students: radial and same at each point on a sphere. Write Gauss: ∮ E·dA = E(r)·4π r². Case 1: r > R. Then Qenc = q. So E·4π r² = q/ε0 → E = q/(4π ε0 r²) r̂. Case 2: r < R. The Gaussian surface encloses no charge, Qenc = 0, so E = 0. Emphasize units: q in C, r in m, gives N/C. Point to the earlier example in the source: 'outside looks like a point charge at centre.'

anticipated_questions: Should we use the formulas we just derived? (yes)
Can we approximate π as 3.14? (yes, but mention calculator okay)
Do we include direction? (yes: radial outward if charge positive)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the two practice problems with given numbers and remind: show units.
teacher_script.heading: Paired practice problems
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Turn to a partner. I'll hand out two quick problems: (1) Compute E at r=0.05 m from a wire with λ = 5.0×10⁻⁷ C/m. (2) Compute E just outside a spherical shell of radius 0.20 m with q = 4.0×10⁻⁶ C. Show units in each step. You have 4 minutes; I'll circulate." After 3 minutes, call time and ask one pair to present their steps for problem (1).

anticipated_questions: Can we memorize the formulas? (yes, but know the derivations)
What exactly is ε0? (permittivity of free space; value if they ask)
Will these be on the test? (yes, derivations expected)
teacher_script.board_action: Underline the three final formulas and add a short checklist: symmetry, Gaussian surface, compute flux, compute Qenc, solve for E, check units.
teacher_script.heading: Check and consolidate; final summary
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Ask: "In one sentence each, tell me the dependence of E on r for the wire, plane, and shell (inside and outside)." Call on three students. Then read the blackboard formulas aloud and say: "These are the results you must be able to derive with Gauss's law. Remember: symmetry chooses your Gaussian surface; units must check out; and edge effects break the ideal results for finite objects." Assign: 'If you finish early, re-derive one of the results at home and check units.'

examples.body: A charged sphere A with charge q and a charged sphere B with charge q' are touched by identical uncharged spheres C and D respectively, so charges redistribute by symmetry to q/2 and q'/2 on each pair. Halving the centre-to-centre separation of A and B changes r to r/2; using Coulomb's law the force becomes (q/2)(q'/2)/(4πε0 (r/2)^2) which equals the original F = q q'/(4πε0 r^2), so the electrostatic force on A due to B remains unaltered.

evidence.quote: When an identical but uncharged sphere C touches A, the charges redistribute on A and C and, by symmetry, each sphere carries a charge q/2. Similarly, after D touches B, the redistributed charge on each is q¢/2.
